questions.problem: Which value of $y$ satisfies the equation $\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}}=\frac{3}{2y}+\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We note that $y=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators ${y}^{2}$ and $2y.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}({y}^{2},2y)=2{y}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2{y}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}} & =\frac{3}{2y}+\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}} \\ 2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}}) & =2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2y}+\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}}) \\ 2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}}) & =2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{3}{2y})+2{y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}}) \\ 2\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{y+1}{{y}^{2}}) & =y\cdot 2y\cdot (\frac{3}{2y})+2\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2y-1}{{y}^{2}}) \\ 2\cdot \cancel{{y}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{y+1}{\cancel{{y}^{2}}}) & =y\cdot \cancel{2y}\cdot (\frac{3}{\cancel{2y}})+2\cdot \cancel{{y}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{2y-1}{\cancel{{y}^{2}}}) \\ 2(y+1) & =3y+2(2y-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $y,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(y+1) & =3y+2(2y-1) \\ 2y+2 & =7y-2 \\ 7y-2y & =2+2 \\ 5y & =4 \\ y & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $y=0$ as a solution. But since $y=\frac{4}{5}\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $y=\frac{4}{5}.$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+1}{2x-1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ For $x\ne \frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{'}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{'}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=2x+\sqrt{x}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(1).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(1),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(1)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(1))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(1).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(1)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(1) & =x \\ f(x) & =1 \\ 2x+\sqrt{x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{x} & =1-2x \\ x & =1-4x+4{x}^{2} \\ 4{x}^{2}-5x+1 & =0 \\ (4x-1)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =\frac{1}{4},\,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Checking the solutions, we notice that only $x=\frac{1}{4}$ satisfies the equation $2x+\sqrt{x}=1.$ Therefore, we discard $x=1$ and conclude that ${f}^{-1}(1)=\frac{1}{4}.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{'}(\frac{1}{4}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =2x+\sqrt{x} \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =2+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}^{'}(\frac{1}{4}) & =2+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{(\frac{1}{4})}} \\ {f}^{'}(\frac{1}{4}) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the polynomial $P(x)$ given that 

$$
2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5=(x-5)(x+1)P(x).
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5.$ We know that $(x+1)$ and $(x-5)$ are factors of $f(x),$ and we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x+1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x+1)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $2$ | $-10$ | $-1$ | $6$ | $-5$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-2$ | $12$ | $-11$ | $5$ |
|  | $2$ | $-12$ | $11$ | $-5$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5}{x+1}=2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+11x-5,
$$

which means that

$$
2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5=(x+1)(2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+11x-5).
$$

Now, because $(x-5)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $(2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+11x-5).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x-5)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $5$ | $2$ | $-12$ | $11$ | $-5$ |
|  | $↓$ | $10$ | $-10$ | $5$ |
|  | $2$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{2{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}+11x-5}{x-5}=2{x}^{2}-2x+1,
$$

which means that

$$
2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5=(x-5)(x+1)(2{x}^{2}-2x+1).
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial $2{x}^{2}-2x+1$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:

$$
{b}^{2}-4ac=(-2)^{2}-4(2)(1)=-4<0
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial $2{x}^{2}-2x+1$ cannot be factored over the real numbers since its discriminant is negative. 

Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ over the real numbers is given by 

$$
2{x}^{4}-10{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+6x-5=(x-5)(x+1){{(2{x}^{2}-2x+1)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}.
$$

Finally, $P(x)=2{x}^{2}-2x+1.$

questions.problem: Find the least common multiple of $6w,$ $3{w}^{3},$ and $4{w}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the least common multiple ($\text{LCM}$) of three monomials, we find the least common multiple of the constants and the least common multiple of the variable parts. Then, we multiply all of the results together.

So first, we find $\text{LCM}(6,3,4):$

- Multiples of $6:$ $\,6,12,18,…$

- Multiples of $3:$ $\,3,6,9,12,…$

- Multiples of $4:$ $\,4,8,12,16,…$

So, $\text{LCM}(6,3,4)=12.$

To find the $\text{LCM}$ of $w,\,{w}^{3},$ and ${w}^{2},$ we raise $w$ to the largest power that appears in all the expressions, which is $3.$ Therefore,

$$
\text{LCM}(w,{w}^{3},{w}^{2})={w}^{3}.
$$

Finally, we multiply all of our results together:

$$
\text{LCM}(6w,3{w}^{3},4{w}^{2})=12\cdot {w}^{3}=12{w}^{3}.
$$

questions.problem: In a right triangle $△XYZ,$ $∠X$ is a right angle, $XZ=\sqrt{5}$ and $YZ=7.$ Find the cosine of $∠Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](images/ea/ea0502e8b261358c7b55c60df02474c5b39a75cbb104d6ba3efb40300294ef56.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}Y=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{XY}{YZ}=\frac{XY}{7}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $XY.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{Y{Z}^{2}-X{Z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{7}^{2}-(\sqrt{5})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{49-5} \\  & =\sqrt{44} \\  & =2\sqrt{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}Y & =\frac{XY}{7}=\frac{2\sqrt{11}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, which of the following is true regarding the series ${\sum }_{n=100}^{\infty }{a}_{n}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Removing the first $k-1$ terms from a convergent series results in a convergent series.

More precisely, assume that $k\ge 1$ is an integer. Then, we have the following:

*If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=k}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.*

So, since ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, we have that ${\sum }_{n=100}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.

Find ${lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(2f(x)+3)^{8}}{(f(x)+4)^{3}}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted above.
questions.worked_solution:
Using the power and quotient rules, we can rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(2f(x)+3)^{8}}{(f(x)+4)^{3}} & =\frac{{({lim}_{x\to 0}(2f(x)+3))}^{8}}{{({lim}_{x\to 0}(f(x)+4))}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The above is true provided that  ${lim}_{x\to 0}f(x)$ exists.

We find from the graph that ${lim}_{x\to 0}f(x)=-2.$ We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}(2f(x)+3)=2(-2)+3=-1
$$

and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}(f(x)+4)=-2+4=2
$$

So we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(2f(x)+3)^{8}}{(f(x)+4)^{3}} & =\frac{{({lim}_{x\to 0}(2f(x)+3))}^{8}}{{({lim}_{x\to 0}(f(x)+4))}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{(-1)^{8}}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\,.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Suppose that $h(t)=90-5{t}^{2}$ represents the height of a ball thrown from the roof of a building, measured in meters from the ground level at $t$ seconds. What is the average rate of loss of height of $h(t)$ from $t=1$ to $t=4?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $h(t)=90-5{t}^{2}$ be the height of the ball, in meters, after $t$ seconds. To find the average rate of change of the ball's height from $t=1$ to $t=4$, we use the average rate of change formula on the interval $[1,4]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δh}{Δt} & =\frac{h(b)-h(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{h(4)-h(1)}{4-1} \\  & =\frac{[90-5(4)^{2}]-[90-5(1)^{2}]}{3} \\  & =\frac{10-85}{3} \\  & =-\frac{75}{3} \\  & =-25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average rate of loss of height of $h(t)$ is $25$ meters per second.

questions.problem: The number of bacteria in culture is given by the function $f(t)=-0.6{t}^{2}+10t+50,$ where $t$ is the time, in minutes, since the bacteria was isolated. What is the average rate of growth of $f(t)$ over the first $10$ minutes?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(t)=-0.6{t}^{2}+10t+50$ be the number of bacteria in the culture after $t$ minutes. To find the average rate of growth of $f(t)$ over the first $10$ minutes, we use the average rate of change formula on the interval $[0,10]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δt} & =\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{f(10)-f(0)}{10-0} \\  & =\frac{[-0.6(10)^{2}+10(10)+50]-[-0.6(0)^{2}+10(0)+50]}{10} \\  & =\frac{90-50}{10} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the average rate of growth over the first $10$ minutes is $4$ bacteria per minute.

questions.problem: Given that $\frac{3y}{2y-1}=a$ and $\frac{1-y}{2(2y-1)}=b,$ what is $a-b?$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3y}{2y-1}-\frac{1-y}{2(2y-1)} & = \\ \frac{2}{2}\cdot \frac{3y}{2y-1}-\frac{1-y}{2(2y-1)} & = \\ \frac{2\cdot 3y}{2(2y-1)}-\frac{1-y}{2(2y-1)} & = \\ \frac{6y}{2(2y-1)}-\frac{1-y}{2(2y-1)} & = \\ \frac{6y-(1-y)}{2(2y-1)} & = \\ \frac{6y-1+y}{2(2y-1)} & = \\ \frac{7y-1}{2(2y-1)} & \end{aligned}

Therefore, $x=-1$ is a valid solution.

questions.problem:
Given that  ${a}_{n}=\frac{5}{(n+1)^{2}}$ for $n\ge 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. - $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1$
II. - ${a}_{n}$ is an increasing sequence
III. - ${a}_{n}$ is a decreasing sequence
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is a positive sequence defined for $n\ge 1,$ and that

$$
L=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}.
$$

Then,

- if $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *increasing,* and

- if $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *decreasing.*

Notice that, in this case, ${a}_{n}=\frac{5}{(n+1)^{2}}$ is positive for all $n\ge 1.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement.

- Statement I is true. Computing the ratio $L,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{5}{(n+2)^{2}})}{(\frac{5}{(n+1)^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{5(n+1)^{2}}{5(n+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(n+1)^{2}}{(n+2)^{2}} \\  & ={(\frac{n+1}{n+2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $n\ge 1,$ it follows that

$$
\frac{n+1}{n+2}<1,
$$

since the numerator is always smaller than the denominator. Therefore,

$$
0<L<1.
$$

- Statement II is false, whereas statement III is true. Since $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ we can conclude that the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following series converge?

I. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}^{3}}}$
II. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{n}^{5}}}$
III. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{\sqrt{{n}^{3}}}$
questions.worked_solution:
We analyze each series in turn.

- First, we look at ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}^{3}}}.$ Rewriting this gives

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{{n}^{3}}}={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{3/2}},
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{3}{2}.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

- For the second series, we have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{n}^{5}}}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{5/4}},
$$

 
which is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{5}{4}.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

- For the third series, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{\sqrt{{n}^{3}}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{{n}^{3/2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{1/2}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{1}{2}.$ Since $p\le 1,$ the series is divergent.

Hence, the correct answer is "I and II only".

- The series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n}$ is a $p$-series with $p=1$ (the harmonic series). Since $p\le 1,$ the series diverges by the $p$-series test.

- The series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{3}}$ is a $p$-series with $p=3.$ Since $p>1,$ the series is convergent by the $p$-series test.

- For the third series, we have

$$

which is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{7}{3}.$ Since $p>1,$ the series is convergent by the $p$-series test.

Hence, the correct answer is "II and III only".

questions.problem: For which values of $q$ does the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{q+1}}$ converge?
questions.worked_solution:
A $p$-series is any series that takes the form

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{p}},
$$

where $p$ is a constant. The $p$-series test states that

- if $p>1,$ then the series converges, while

- if $p\le 1,$ then the series diverges.

Comparing our series to the $p$-series, we have

$$
p=q+1.
$$

According to the $p$-series test, the given series converges if

$$
q+1>1\,⟹\,q>0.
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent for all $q>0.$

questions.problem: Let $A$ and $B$ be the set of all multiples of $4$ greater than $0$ and the set of all multiples of $5$ greater than $0,$ respectively. What is $A\cup B?$

$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the vertical asymptote of the function $f(x)={log}_{3}(4x+1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of the vertical asymptote of the function $y={log}_{3}x$ is $x=0.$

To find the equation of the vertical asymptote of $f(x)$, we set the argument of the logarithmic term equal to zero, and solve for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+1 & =0 \\ 4x & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the vertical asymptote is $x=-\frac{1}{4}.$

questions.problem: Find the root of $f(x)={log}_{2}(3x-1)-3.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
{log}_{2}(3x-1)-3=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}(3x-1)-3 & =0 \\ {log}_{2}(3x-1) & =3 \\ {2}^{{log}_{2}(3x-1)} & ={2}^{3} \\ 3x-1 & =8 \\ 3x & =9 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=3.$

questions.problem: Calculate the discriminant of the quadratic equation $2(x+2)^{2}-3=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}2(x+2)^{2}-3 & =2({x}^{2}+4x+{2}^{2})-3 \\  & =2{x}^{2}+8x+8-3 \\  & =2{x}^{2}+8x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

We have $a=2,$ $b=8,$ and $c=5.$ So, we calculate the discriminant as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & ={8}^{2}-4(2)(5) \\  & =64-40 \\  & =24\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the equation $-{x}^{2}-2x+7=0.$ How many distinct real solutions does it have?
questions.worked_solution:
To quickly determine the number of solutions, we can compute the discriminant. We have $a=-1,$ $b=-2,$ and $c=7,$ so the discriminant is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(-2)^{2}-4(-1)(7) \\  & =4+28 \\  & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Since the discriminant is positive $(D>0),$ the equation has two distinct real solutions.

questions.problem: Consider the equation $-5{x}^{2}+2x-6=0.$ How many distinct real solutions does it have?

$$

$$

Since the discriminant is negative $(D<0),$ the equation has no real solutions.

questions.problem: Consider the equation ${x}^{2}-4x+5=0.$ How many distinct real solutions does it have?

questions.problem:
Which of the following series are convergent?

I. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{4n}$
II. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}\sqrt{n}}$
III. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{3{n}^{5}}$
questions.worked_solution:
We analyze each series in turn.

- First, we look at ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{4n}.$ Rewriting this series gives

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{4n}=\frac{1}{4}\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n},
$$

 
which is a $p$-series with $p=1$ (the harmonic series). Since $p\le 1,$ the series is divergent.

- For the second series, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}\sqrt{n}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}\cdot {n}^{1/2}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{5/2}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{5}{2}.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

- For the third series, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{3{n}^{5}} & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{5}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=5.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

Hence, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem: According to the rational roots theorem, which of the following **cannot** be a root of the polynomial $f(x)=2{x}^{3}+5{x}^{2}+x-3?$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-3$ and the leading coefficient is $2.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-3}{\text{factor of }2}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $2$ does not take the above form. The value $2$ can be interpreted as a fraction $\frac{2}{1},$ and the numerator $(2)$ is not a factor of $-3.$

questions.problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-10x+8$ has one of its roots in the interval $(-5,-1),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $8$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }8}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 4,\pm 8
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-5,-1),$ are $-4$ and $-2.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-10$ | $8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-4$ | $12$ | $-8$ |
|  | $1$ | $-3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+4)({x}^{2}-3x+2) \\  & =(x+4)(x-1)(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-4,1,2.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-4+1+2=-1.
$$

questions.problem:
Two fair $6$-sided dice are rolled. Define $A$ to be the event "the sum of outcomes is equal to $5.$" Which of the following statements are true regarding this event?

I. - $P(A)=0.15$ to $2$ decimal places
II. - ${A}^{'}$ is the event "the sum of the outcomes is less than $5$"
III. - $P({A}^{'})=0.89$ to $2$ decimal places
questions.worked_solution:
Let's inspect each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. There are $36$ possible outcomes and $4$ of these have the sum of the outcomes equal to $5,$ namely $(1,4),(4,1),(2,3),(3,2).$ Therefore,

$$
P(A)=\frac{4}{36}=0.11
$$

to $2$ decimal places.

- Statement II is false. The complement of $A$ is the event ${A}^{'},$ "the sum of the outcomes is not equal to $5.$

- Statement III is true. Since we know that $P(A)=0.11$ to $2$ decimal places, we can calculate $P({A}^{'})$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A)+P({A}^{'}) & =1 \\ P({A}^{'}) & =1-P(A) \\  & =1-0.11 \\  & =0.89.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem: Given an arithmetic sequence that has $f(2)=5$ and $f(4)=23$, what is the index of the term $158?$
questions.worked_solution:
To construct the formula for the sequence, we need to know the common difference $d$ and the first term $f(1).$

Since we are given $f(2)=5$ and $f(4)=23,$ we can find the common difference by dividing the total difference by the number of jumps:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{f(4)-f(2)}{4-2} \\  & =\frac{23-5}{4-2} \\  & =\frac{18}{2} \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(2)=5$ is $1$ jump after $f(1),$ we can determine the first term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =f(1)+d \\ 5 & =f(1)+9 \\ -4 & =f(1)\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)+(n-1)d \\  & =-4+(n-1)(9) \\  & =-4+9n-9 \\  & =9n-13\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for the value of $n$ that gives $f(n)=158,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =9n-13 \\ 158 & =9n-13 \\ 171 & =9n \\ \frac{171}{9} & =n \\ 19 & =n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $158$ is the $19$th term of the sequence.

questions.problem: Let $E$ and $F$ be the set of all non-negative integer powers of $2$ and the set of all non-negative integer powers of $4,$ respectively. What is $E\cap F?$
questions.worked_solution:
The powers of $2$ that are greater or equal to $1$ are

$$
E={1,2,4,8,16,32,64,…}.
$$

Likewise, the powers of $4$ that are greater or equal to $1$ are

$$
F={1,4,16,64,256,…}.
$$

Now, $E\cap F$ is the *intersection* of $E$ and $F,$ which means that we want to find the elements that are in *both* $E$ and $F.$ In other words, $E\cap F$ denotes the set of natural numbers that are both, power of $2$ and power of $4.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E\cap F & ={1,2,4,8,16,32,64,…}\cap {1,4,16,64,256,…} \\  & ={1,4,16,64,256,…}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Compute the variance ${\sigma }^{2}$ of a data set ${x}_{i}$ consisting of $9$ data points, where

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{9}{x}_{i}=27,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{9}{x}_{i}^{2}=117.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If we have a data set that consists of the points ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n},$ then the variance of the data set is given by 

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}-(\overset{―}{x})^{2},
$$

where $\overset{―}{x}$ is the mean of the data set and $\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}$ is the mean of the squares of the points in the data set.

First, let's compute $\overset{―}{x}.$ There are $n=9$ points in our data set, and we know that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{9}{x}_{i}=27,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{x} & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{\sum }_{i=1}^{9}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot 27 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's compute $\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}.$ We know that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{9}{x}_{i}^{2}=117,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{{x}^{2}} & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{\sum }_{i=1}^{9}{x}_{i}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot 117 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\overset{―}{{x}^{2}}-(\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =13-{(3)}^{2} \\  & =13-9 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Solve the inequality $3-2\sqrt{2x+8}>-9.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the square root:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-2\sqrt{2x+8} & >-9 \\ -2\sqrt{2x+8} & >-12 \\ \sqrt{2x+8} & <6\end{aligned}
$$

In this inequality, the square root is being compared to a non-negative number $(6).$ So, we can square both sides of the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\sqrt{2x+8})}^{2} & <{6}^{2} \\ 2x+8 & <36 \\ 2x & <28 \\ x & <14\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the square root. To find the domain of the square root, we recall that the argument of the square root must be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+8 & \ge 0 \\ 2x & \ge -8 \\ x & \ge -4\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x<14,$ which can be expressed as $(-\infty ,14).$ But the domain of the square root is $x\ge -4,$ which can be expressed as $[-4,\infty ).$ To find the solutions that are in the domain of the square root, we take the intersection:

$$
(-\infty ,14)\cap [-4,\infty )=[-4,14)
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [-4,14),$ which can also be written as $-4\le x<14.$

questions.problem: What is the product of solutions of the equation $4{x}^{2}{e}^{5x}=3{e}^{5x}-4x{e}^{5x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}{e}^{5x} & =3{e}^{5x}-4x{e}^{5x} \\ 4{x}^{2}{e}^{5x}+4x{e}^{5x}-3{e}^{5x} & =0 \\ (4{x}^{2}+4x-3){e}^{5x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
4{x}^{2}+4x-3=0\,\text{and}\,{e}^{5x}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation $4{x}^{2}+4x-3=0$ can be factored as

$$
(2x+3)(2x-1)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}.$

- The equation ${e}^{5x}=0$ has no solutions because ${e}^{5x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, the original equation has the solutions $x=-\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2},$ and their product is $(-\frac{3}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{3}{4}.$

questions.problem: Find the root of $f(x)=2(5)^{3x+2}-54.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
2(5)^{3x+2}-54=0
$$

First, we isolate the term with the variable exponent by adding $54$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2(5)^{3x+2}-54 & =0 \\ 2(5)^{3x+2}-\cancel{54}+\cancel{54} & =0+54 \\ 2(5)^{3x+2} & =54\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing both sides by $2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(5)^{3x+2} & =54 \\ {5}^{3x+2} & =27.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we rewrite $27$ as ${3}^{3}$ to get

$$
{5}^{3x+2}={3}^{3}.
$$

Then we take ${log}_{5}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{3x+2} & ={3}^{3} \\ {log}_{5}({5}^{3x+2}) & ={log}_{5}({3}^{3}) \\ 3x+2 & =3{log}_{5}(3)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2 & =3{log}_{5}(3) \\ 3x & =3{log}_{5}(3)-2 \\ x & =\frac{3{log}_{5}(3)-2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the root of $f(x)=3\sqrt[6]{3x+13}-6.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
3\sqrt[6]{3x+13}-6=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\sqrt[6]{3x+13}-6 & =0 \\ 3\sqrt[6]{3x+13} & =6 \\ \sqrt[6]{3x+13} & =2 \\ (\sqrt[6]{3x+13})^{6} & ={2}^{6} \\ 3x+13 & =64 \\ 3x & =51 \\ x & =17\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we must check the answer by substituting it back into the initial equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\sqrt[6]{3\cdot 17+13}-6 & =0 \\ 3\sqrt[6]{64}-6 & =0 \\ 3\cdot 2-6 & =0 \\ 0 & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=17.$

questions.worked_solution:

questions.problem:
Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

I. - $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x={e}^{y}$
II. - $y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2=\sqrt{y}$
III. - $4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{x}{y}=5y$
questions.worked_solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x & ={e}^{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={e}^{y}+x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)={e}^{y}+x.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

- Equation II is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2 & =\sqrt{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\sqrt{y}+2}{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\frac{\sqrt{y}+2}{2}.$

- Equation III is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{x}{y} & =5y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{4}(5y+\frac{x}{y}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{4}(5y+\frac{x}{y}).$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

I. - $x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{y}^{3}=2$
II. - $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-7{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{y}$
III. - $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{ln}y$
questions.worked_solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{y}^{3} & =2 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2+3{y}^{3}}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{2+3{y}^{3}}{x}.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

- Equation II is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-7{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =7{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=7{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{y}.$

- Equation III is an autonomous differential equation. We see that it is of the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ where $f(y)=\operatorname{ln}y.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

I. - ${e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{y}^{3}=0$
II. - $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x=\operatorname{ln}y$
III. - $5x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x}=0$
questions.worked_solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3{y}^{3} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{y}^{3}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=3{y}^{3}{e}^{-y}.$

- Equation II is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-2x & =\operatorname{ln}y \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}y+2x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}y+2x.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

- Equation III is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}5x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y}{5{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{5{x}^{2}}.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following are **not** autonomous ordinary differential equations?

I. - ${y}^{'}=1-\sqrt{y}$
II. - ${y}^{'}-\operatorname{tan}y={e}^{2}$
III. - $x{y}^{'}-\frac{1}{y}=4$
questions.worked_solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is an autonomous differential equation. It is of the form ${y}^{'}=f(y),$ where $f(y)=1-\sqrt{y}.$

- Equation II is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form ${y}^{'}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'}-\operatorname{tan}y & ={e}^{2} \\ {y}^{'} & =\operatorname{tan}y+{e}^{2} \\ {y}^{'} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\operatorname{tan}y+{e}^{2}.$

- Equation III is *not* an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{'}-\frac{1}{y} & =4 \\ {y}^{'} & =\frac{4y+1}{xy} \\ {y}^{'} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{4y+1}{xy}.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

A first-order initial value problem (or IVP) is a first-order ordinary differential equation together with an initial condition that specifies a value of the unknown function at a point in its domain. A first-order initial value problem typically takes the form

$$
{y}^{'}=f(x,y),\,y({x}_{0})={y}_{0},
$$

where ${x}_{0}$ and ${y}_{0}$ are constants.

With that in mind, let's check each option.

- System I is not a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a *second*-order differential equation ${x}^{2}{y}^{''}-y=2x$ together with *two* initial conditions $y(1)=1,\,{y}^{'}(1)=3.$ This is a second-order initial value problem.

- System II is not a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a *third*-order differential equation $x{y}^{‴}-{e}^{x}{y}^{'}=9y$ together with *three* initial conditions $y(0)=1,\,{y}^{'}(0)=1,$ and ${y}^{''}(0)=2.$ This is a third-order initial value problem.

- System III is a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a first-order differential equation $2{y}^{'}-\frac{1}{x}={e}^{y}$ together with the initial condition $y(0)=1.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem:
Consider the following trigonometric equation: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}(\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{\pi }{3})=-1
$$

 

The general solution of this equation can be expressed as

$$
x=b\pi +6n\pi ,
$$

where $n$ is any integer. Which of the following could be the value of $b?$
questions.worked_solution:
The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{\pi }{3} & =-\frac{\pi }{2}+2n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation above for $x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{2}+2n\pi  \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+2n\pi  \\ x & =-\frac{\pi }{2}+6n\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that $b=-\frac{1}{2}.$

questions.problem: Evaluate $\frac{7}{\operatorname{log}(100)}-\operatorname{log}(1\,000).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite $100$ and $1\,000$ as a power of $10$ (the base of the common logarithm) as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & ={10}^{2} \\ 1\,000 & ={10}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
\frac{7}{\operatorname{log}(100)}-\operatorname{log}(1\,000)=\frac{7}{\operatorname{log}({10}^{2})}-\operatorname{log}({10}^{3})
$$

The common logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{log}({10}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=2$ and $x=3.$ Therefore:

$$
\frac{7}{\operatorname{log}({10}^{2})}-\operatorname{log}({10}^{3})=\frac{7}{2}-3=\frac{1}{2}
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${e}^{6w+3}+7=11,$ then $w=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation into a form that is more convenient for logarithms, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{6w+3}+7=11 \\ {e}^{6w+3} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the natural logarithm $(ln)$ of both sides of the equation and solve for $w:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{6w+3} & =4 \\ \operatorname{ln}({e}^{6w+3}) & =\operatorname{ln}(4) \\ 6w+3 & =\operatorname{ln}(4) \\ 6w & =\operatorname{ln}(4)-3 \\ w & =\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{ln}(4)-3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $w=\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{ln}(4)-3).$

questions.problem: If ${log}_{8}x+2{log}_{8}x=2$, then what is the value of  $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}x+2{log}_{8}x & =2 \\ (1+2){log}_{8}x & =2 \\ 3{log}_{8}x & =2 \\ {log}_{8}x & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $8,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}x & =\frac{2}{3} \\ {8}^{{log}_{8}x} & ={8}^{2/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${8}^{{log}_{8}x}=x.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={8}^{2/3} \\ x & =\sqrt[3]{64} \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $2,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}x & =\frac{1}{7} \\ {2}^{{log}_{2}x} & ={2}^{1/7}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${2}^{{log}_{2}x}=x.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={2}^{1/7} \\ x & =\sqrt[7]{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find $x$ such that $\operatorname{ln}(8x)=10.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}(8x) & =10 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}(8x)} & ={e}^{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}(8x)}=8x.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}8x & ={e}^{10} \\ x & =\frac{1}{8}{e}^{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use a calculator to evaluate ${log}_{18}(41)$ rounded to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's calculate ${log}_{18}(41)$ by changing the base $18$ to the common logarithm (base $10$).

We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}X=\frac{{log}_{b}X}{{log}_{b}a}
$$

In our case, $a=18,$ $X=41,$ $b=10.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{18}(41) & =\frac{{log}_{10}(41)}{{log}_{10}(18)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{log}(41)}{\operatorname{log}(18)} \\  & \approx \frac{1.612\,784}{1.255\,273} \\  & \approx 1.285\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Solve the equation $\operatorname{log}(x-2)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{log}(256).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we use the power rule to simplify the right-hand side. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{log}(256) \\ \operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\operatorname{log}({256}^{1/4}) \\ \operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\operatorname{log}(4).\end{aligned}
$$

Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\operatorname{log}(4) \\ x-2 & =4 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation: 

- Substituting $x=6$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}(x-2) & =\operatorname{log}(6-2) \\  & =\operatorname{log}(4) \\  & =\operatorname{log}({256}^{1/4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{log}(256).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=6$ is a valid solution.

questions.problem: If $4\operatorname{ln}x-2=10,$ what is the value of $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{ln}x-2 & =10 \\ 4\operatorname{ln}x & =12 \\ \operatorname{ln}x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The logarithm is a natural logarithm, which means its base is $e.$ So, we use a base of $e$ for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}x & =3 \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}x} & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${e}^{\operatorname{ln}x}=x.$ 

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={e}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}({v}^{2}+36) & ={log}_{5}(-16v-28) \\ {v}^{2}+36 & =-16v-28 \\ {v}^{2}+16v+64 & =0 \\ (v+8)^{2} & =0 \\ v & =-8.\end{aligned}

- Substituting $v=-8$ back into the original equation, we get

$$

Therefore, $v=-8$ is a valid solution.

questions.problem: Let $A(6,7,6)$ and $B(8,9,5).$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $\overset{\to }{AB}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=6i+7j+6k, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=8i+9j+5k.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing $\overset{\to }{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{OB}-\overset{\to }{OA} \\  & =b-a \\  & =8i+9j+5k-(6i+7j+6k) \\  & =2i+2j-k \\  & =⟨2,2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector, we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
u=\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{|\,\overset{\to }{AB}\,|}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,\overset{\to }{AB}\,| & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $\overset{\to }{AB}$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{|\,\overset{\to }{AB}\,|} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\overset{\to }{AB} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot ⟨2,2,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3},-\frac{1}{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{4x-3}-3}{x-3} & =\frac{\sqrt{4(3)-3}-3}{3-3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{9}-3}{3-3} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{4x-3}-3}{x-3} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(\sqrt{4x-3}-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(\sqrt{4x-3})^{2}-{3}^{2}}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{4x-3-9}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{4x-12}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{4(x-3)}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{4}{\sqrt{4x-3}+3} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{4(3)-3}+3} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{9}+3} \\  & =\frac{4}{6} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{5x+6}-4}{x-2} & =\frac{\sqrt{5(2)+6}-4}{2-2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{16}-4}{2-2} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{5x+6}-4}{x-2} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(\sqrt{5x+6}-4)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(\sqrt{5x+6})^{2}-{4}^{2}}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{5x+6-16}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{5x-10}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{5(x-2)}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{5}{\sqrt{5x+6}+4} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{5(2)+6}+4} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{16}+4} \\  & =\frac{5}{4+4} \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: ${lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{3x+4}-2}=$
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=0,$ we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{3x+4}-2} & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{3(0)+4}-2} \\  & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{4}-2} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{3x+4}-2} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{3x+4}+2)}{(\sqrt{3x+4}-2)(\sqrt{3x+4}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{3x+4}+2)}{(\sqrt{3x+4})^{2}-{2}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{3x+4}+2)}{3x+4-4} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{3x+4}+2)}{3x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{3x+4}+2}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3(0)+4}+2}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4}+2}{3} \\  & =\frac{2+2}{3} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we expand the parentheses on the right-hand-side:

$$
\begin{aligned}p+2 & =3(p-3)+6 \\ p+2 & =3\cdot p-3\cdot 3+6 \\ p+2 & =3p-9+6 \\ p+2 & =3p-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must now bring all variables to one side of the equation and all constants to the other side. 

Notice that we have $p$ on the left-hand side and $3p$ on the right-hand side. Since the variable on the right-hand side has a larger coefficient, let's bring all the variables to this side. 

The first step is to remove the $p$ from the left-hand side of the equation. We do this by subtracting $p$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}p+2 & =3p-3 \\ p+2-p & =3p-3-p \\ 2 & =2p-3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we remove the $-3$ from the right-hand side. We do this by adding $3$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2p-3 \\ 2+3 & =2p-3+3 \\ 5 & =2p\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2} & =\frac{2p}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2} & =\frac{\cancel{2}p}{\cancel{2}} \\ \frac{5}{2} & =p \\ p & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $y=7-4{log}_{3}x$, find the instantaneous rate of change at $x=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To differentiate a logarithm with base $a,$ we use the formula

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{a}x)=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}a}.
$$

To find the instantaneous rate of change at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7-4{log}_{3}x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(7)-4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{3}x) \\  & =0-4\cdot \frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}3} \\  & =-\frac{4}{x\operatorname{ln}3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=1/\operatorname{ln}3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1/\operatorname{ln}3} & ={(-\frac{4}{x\operatorname{ln}3})\,|}_{x=1/\operatorname{ln}3} \\  & =-\frac{4}{1} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $y=4{e}^{x}-3{log}_{7}x$, find the slope of the tangent at $x=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4{e}^{x}-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}7}\,.
$$

Therefore, the slope  of the tangent at $x=3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=3} & ={(4{e}^{x}-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}7})|}_{x=3} \\  & =4{e}^{3}-\frac{3}{3\operatorname{ln}7} \\  & =4{e}^{3}-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}7}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for the average rate of change, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \\  & =\frac{f(5)-f(-5)}{5-(-5)} \\  & =\frac{(p+6)-(4p+1)}{5+5} \\  & =\frac{5-3p}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we know that $\frac{Δf}{Δx}=-1$ on the interval $[-5,5].$ Thus, 

$$
\frac{5-3p}{10}=-1.
$$

Solving for $p,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5-3p}{10} & =-1 \\ 5-3p & =-10 \\ -3p & =-10-5 \\ -3p & =-15 \\ p & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $y=\frac{1}{4x},$ find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first rewrite the function as

$$
y=\frac{1}{4x}=\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-1}.
$$

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{d}{dx}(\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot (-1){x}^{-1-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate $v(t)$ to calculate $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2-3t}) \\  & =-3\cdot {e}^{2-3t}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
What is the fourth term of the following sequence?

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n)\,,\,f(1)=-2\,,\,f(2)=0,\,n\ge 1
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The fourth term is represented by $f(4).$

To compute $f(4),$ we first need to compute $f(3).$ So, we substitute $n=1$ into the recursive formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n+2) & =f(n+1)+f(1) \\ f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =0+(-2) \\ f(3) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to compute $f(4),$ we substitute $n=2$ into the recursive formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+2) & =f(2+1)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =f(3)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =-2+0 \\ f(4) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fourth term of the sequence is $f(4)=-2.$

The recursive formula is

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n).
$$

Substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =1+(-1) \\ f(3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(3)=0.$

To compute $f(4),$ we first need to compute $f(3).$ So, we substitute $n=1$ into the recursive formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n+2) & =f(n+1)+f(1) \\ f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =2+0 \\ f(3) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to compute $f(4),$ we substitute $n=2$ into the recursive formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+2) & =f(2+1)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =f(3)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =2+2 \\ f(4) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(4)=4.$

questions.problem: Consider the sequence starting from ${a}_{1}=\frac{6}{5}$  with the property $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=\frac{3}{4}$ for all $n\ge 1.$ Write the sum to infinity of the terms of this sequence using sigma notation.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the sequence is a geometric sequence since the ratio of any two successive terms is constant.

The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=\frac{6}{5},$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the general term ${a}_{n}$ can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}{(r)}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{-1}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the infinite geometric series can be written in sigma notation as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{8}{5}){(\frac{3}{4})}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{10}{3-{x}^{2}}$, find ${f}^{'}(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
The numerator and denominator are $u(x)=10$ and $v(x)=3-{x}^{2},$ respectively. Their derivatives are given by

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{'}(x) & =0, \\ {v}^{'}(x) & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(0)\cdot (3-{x}^{2})-(10)\cdot (-2x)}{{(3-{x}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{20x}{{(3-{x}^{2})}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{3-2x}{2{x}^{2}-2}$, find ${f}^{'}(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
The numerator and denominator are $u(x)=3-2x$ and $v(x)=2{x}^{2}-2,$ respectively. Their derivatives are given by

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{'}(x) & =-2, \\ {v}^{'}(x) & =4x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the quotient rule, we have

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{'}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{'}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-2)(2{x}^{2}-2)-(3-2x)(4x)}{{(2{x}^{2}-2)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-4{x}^{2}+4-12x+8{x}^{2}}{{(2{x}^{2}-2)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{2}-12x+4}{4{({x}^{2}-1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}-3x+1}{{({x}^{2}-1)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find ${f}^{'}(x)$ if $f(x)={e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We calculate the derivative using the product rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}x) \\  & ={e}^{x}(\operatorname{csc}x)+{e}^{x}(-\operatorname{csc}x\operatorname{cot}x) \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{csc}x(1-\operatorname{cot}x)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ if $f(x)=x\operatorname{cot}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the derivative using the product rule:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{cot}x) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}x+x(-{csc}^{2}x) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}x-x{csc}^{2}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ in the derivative and get

 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{\pi /4} & =\operatorname{cot}(\frac{\pi }{4})-\frac{\pi }{4}{csc}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot (\sqrt{2})^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{{t}^{7}}}={t}^{n},$ what is $n?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we use that $\frac{1}{{t}^{7}}={t}^{-7}$, then we convert the radical to a fractional exponent, and finally, we apply the power rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{{t}^{7}}} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{{t}^{-7}} & = \\ {({t}^{-7})}^{1/3} & = \\ {t}^{(-7)\cdot (1/3)} & = \\ {t}^{-7/3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $n=-\frac{7}{3}.$

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above? 

I. - ${lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)=-1$
II. - ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=3$
III. - ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. As $x$ approaches $-2,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-2}f(x)=1.
$$

- Statement II is true. As $x$ approaches $0,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=3.$ Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=3.
$$

- Statement III is false. As $x$ approaches $-1,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=2,$ and consequently 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=2.
$$

 
Similarly, as $x$ approaches $2,$ the function $f(x)$ approaches the value $y=1,$ and consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=1.
$$

 As a result,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x).
$$

In conclusion, only statement II is true.

questions.problem: ${lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{\sqrt{x-1}-2}{x-5}=$
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{\sqrt{x-1}-2}{x-5} & =\frac{\sqrt{5-1}-2}{5-5}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{\sqrt{x-1}-2}{x-5} & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{(\sqrt{x-1}-2)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)}{(x-5)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{{(\sqrt{x-1})}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x-5)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{x-1-4}{(x-5)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{x-5}{(x-5)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5-1}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $f(x)=\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x-2}{4-{x}^{2}},$ which of the following statements is correct?

I. - ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)=-\infty $
II. - ${lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}f(x)=\infty $
III. - ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)=-\infty $
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's factor the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x-2}{4-{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{(x+2)(2x-1)}{(x-2)(x+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is  $x\ne \pm 2,$ and we notice that the function can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=-\frac{2x-1}{x-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we see that the function has the only vertical asymptote $x=2.$ So statement II is false.

To find  ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x),$ we evaluate $f(x)$ at $x$-values very close to $x=2$ from the left and right.

| $x$ | $1.99$ | $1.999$ | $2$ | $2.001$ | $2.01$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $298$ | $2\,998$ | $\text{undefined}$ | $-3\,002$ | $-302$ |

All values are positive and get larger and larger as $x\to 2$ from the left and all values are negative and get smaller and smaller as $x\to 2$ from the right . Therefore, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)=-\infty \,{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)=\infty 
$$

Consequently, statement I is true and III is false.

In conclusion, only statement I is correct. A plot of the function is shown below.

![](images/9e/9e96d6a81813c1c89a498d0206234f2685f0a53c1bab626ce7430d84f9c0f506.png)

First, we express $y={e}^{1-3x}$ as the composite function

$$
y={e}^{u},\,u=1-3x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-3{e}^{u} \\  & =-3{e}^{1-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the sum rule of differentiation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{e}^{1-3x}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-(-3{e}^{1-3x}) \\  & =3({x}^{2}+{e}^{1-3x}).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f={2}^{u},\,u=3-{x}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}={2}^{u}\operatorname{ln}2,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{x}^{2}.

We now apply the chain rule, and get

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}(4-2x)$ at the point $(1,\operatorname{ln}2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=\operatorname{ln}u,\,u=4-2x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u}\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{1}{4-2x}\cdot (-2) \\  & =-\frac{2}{4-2x} \\  & =-\frac{\cancel{2}}{\cancel{2}\cdot (2-x)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2-x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent line at the point where $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={-\frac{1}{2-x}|}_{x=1}=-\frac{1}{2-1}=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the slope of the tangent line at the point $(1,\operatorname{ln}2)$ is $m=-1.$ Now, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-\operatorname{ln}2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+\operatorname{ln}2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Express $z=\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}\theta ).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-1-\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1+\text{i})(-1-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1)^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =3(-1-\text{i}) \\  & =-3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=-3-3\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}(z).$ Since $x=-3$ and $y=-3$ are both negative, $z$ lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}(z) & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}|\frac{-3}{-3}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}1 \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=3\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{4}))
$$

questions.problem: The cubic polynomial $f(x)$ has roots ${x}_{1}=-2,{x}_{2,3}=1\pm 2\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $3.$ Find $f(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x)$ has roots ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2,3}=1\pm 2\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $a=3,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2})(x-{x}_{3}) \\  & =3(x-(-2))(x-(1+2\text{i}))(x-(1-2\text{i})) \\  & =3(x+2)(x-(1+2\text{i}))(x-(1-2\text{i}))\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the parentheses, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3(x+2)(x-(1+2\text{i}))(x-(1-2\text{i})) & = \\ 3(x+2)({x}^{2}-x(1+2\text{i})-x(1-2\text{i})+(1+2\text{i})(1-2\text{i})) & = \\ 3(x+2)({x}^{2}-2x+5) & = \\ 3({x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-2{x}^{2}-4x+5x+10) & = \\ 3({x}^{3}+x+10) & = \\ 3{x}^{3}+3x+30 & .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=3{x}^{3}+3x+30.$

questions.problem:
Express the following arithmetic series using sigma notation.

$$
2+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{3}{2}+…-\frac{41}{4}-12
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The first term ${a}_{1}=2$ and the common difference is:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-2 \\  & =-\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =2+(n-1)(-\frac{7}{4}) \\  & =2-\frac{7}{4}n+\frac{7}{4} \\  & =\frac{15}{4}-\frac{7}{4}n\end{aligned}
$$

We don't know the index of the last term, but we can find it using the formula for the $n$th term:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =-12 \\ \frac{15}{4}-\frac{7}{4}n & =-12 \\ \frac{7}{4}n & =\frac{15}{4}+12 \\ \frac{7}{4}n & =\frac{63}{4} \\ n & =9\end{aligned}
$$

There are $9$ terms in total, from $n=1$ to $n=9.$ So, the sigma notation for the given sum is:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{9}(\frac{15}{4}-\frac{7}{4}n)
$$

questions.problem:
Find the sum of the following arithmetic series.

$$
5+11+17+23+⋯+83
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the sum of an arithmetic series, we use the formula

$$
{S}_{N}=\frac{N}{2}({a}_{1}+{a}_{N}),
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term, ${a}_{N}$ is the last term, and $N$ is the total number of terms.

For our series, we have ${a}_{1}=5$ and the common difference is:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =11-5 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =5+(n-1)(6) \\  & =5+6n-6 \\  & =6n-1\end{aligned}
$$

As we know, the last term is ${a}_{N}=83.$ Putting this value in the formula for the $n$th term obtained above, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{N} & =6N-1 \\ 83 & =6N-1 \\ 84 & =6N \\ N & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting ${a}_{1}=5$, ${a}_{14}=83$, and $N=14$ into the formula for ${S}_{N}$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{14} & =\frac{14}{2}(5+83) \\  & =7\cdot 88 \\  & =616\end{aligned}
$$

$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =-14+(n-1)(-6) \\  & =-14-6n+6 \\  & =-6n-8\end{aligned}
$$

As we know, the last term is ${a}_{N}=-314.$ Putting this value in the formula for the $n$th term obtained above, we get:

$$

$$

questions.problem:

$$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the sum of an arithmetic series, we use the formula

$$
{S}_{N}=\frac{N}{2}(2{a}_{1}+(N-1)d),
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term, $d$ is the common difference, and $N$ is the number of terms.

We are given the total number of terms $N=20$ and the first term is ${a}_{1}=13.$ Now, the common difference $d$ can be found as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}d & ={a}_{2}-{a}_{1} \\  & =17-13 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${a}_{1}=13$, $d=4$, and $N=20$ into the above formula for ${S}_{N}$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{20} & =\frac{N}{2}(2{a}_{1}+(N-1)d) \\  & =\frac{20}{2}(2\cdot 13+(20-1)\cdot 4) \\  & =\frac{20}{2}\cdot (26+76) \\  & =\frac{20}{2}\cdot 102 \\  & =10\cdot 102 \\  & =1\,020\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{S}_{N}=\frac{N}{2}(2{a}_{1}+(N-1)d),
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term, $d$ is the common difference, and $N$ is the number of terms.

We are given the total number of terms $N=15$ and the first term is ${a}_{1}=-1.$ Now, the common difference $d$ can be found as follows: 

$$

questions.problem:
Stephanie is a geologist who began studying land subsidence due to a geological fault. The table below shows the land subsidence  $C,$ in centimeters, $n$ weeks after the study began. How many centimeters of subsidence were there at the beginning of the study?

| $n$ (weeks) | $10$ | $15$ | $20$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $C$ (centimeters) | $11$ | $13.5$ | $16$ |

You may assume that the relationship between $n$ and $C$ is linear.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the number of centimeters increases by $2.5$ every $5$ weeks. In other words, the number of centimeters increases by

$$
\frac{2.5}{5}=0.5
$$

centimeters per week. Thus, if $A$ is the amount of subsidence at the beginning of the study, then we can model the total subsidence $C$ after $n$ weeks using the equation

$$
C=A+0.5n.
$$

 

Now, we substitute one of the pairs of values from the table into this equation and solve for $A.$ After $n=10$ weeks the subsidence was $C=11$ centimeters. We substitute these values into the equation and solve for $A,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =A+0.5n \\ 11 & =A+0.5(10) \\ 11 & =A+5 \\ A & =6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, there were $6$ centimeters of subsidence when the study began.

questions.problem: Calculate ${log}_{125}(625)$ without using a calculator.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}X=\frac{{log}_{b}X}{{log}_{b}a}
$$

In our case, $a=125,$ and $X=625.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ are powers of $5,$ we set $b=5.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{125}(625) & =\frac{{log}_{5}(625)}{{log}_{5}(125)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{5}({5}^{4})}{{log}_{5}({5}^{3})} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for ${x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}(y)=8{x}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}(y)$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}(y) & =8{x}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}(y)) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8{x}^{3}) \\ [({x}^{2})(\frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{dy}}{\text{d}x})+(2x)(\operatorname{ln}(y))] & =24{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})+2x\operatorname{ln}(y) & =24{x}^{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{y}(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}) & =24{x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}(y) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{y(24{x}^{2}-2x\operatorname{ln}(y))}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =24y-\frac{2y\operatorname{ln}(y)}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for ${x}^{2}y-4{y}^{3}=8x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $x,$ assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}y$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y-4{y}^{3} & =8x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y-4{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8x) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}y)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8x) \\ [{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy]-12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8 \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2xy-12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now we solve the equation for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-12{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =8-2xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-12{y}^{2}) & =8-2xy \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{8-2xy}{{x}^{2}-12{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{1}{2},\,2)$ for the curve ${x}^{2}{y}^{3}=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope at a point, we use implicit differentiation to calculate the derivative of the curve, assuming that $y=y(x).$

Note that to differentiate the ${x}^{2}{y}^{3}$ term, we will need to use the product rule.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2) \\ {x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{3})+{y}^{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{y}^{3}\cdot 2x & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{y}^{3} & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x{y}^{3}}{3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2y}{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

The slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{1}{2},\,2)$ is then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(1/2,\,2)} \\  & ={(-\frac{2y}{3x})}_{(1/2,\,2)} \\  & =-\frac{2\cdot 2}{3\cdot (\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The position $x$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by $x(t)=t{e}^{t}.$ Calculate the velocity at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The velocity is the derivative of the position function $x(t)$ with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t{e}^{t}) \\  & ={e}^{t}+t{e}^{t} \\  & =(t+1){e}^{t}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle (in millimeters) at time $t$ seconds is given by 

$$
s(t)=9t-{t}^{3},\,t\ge 0.
$$

Calculate the speed of the particle when $t=2\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(9t-{t}^{3}) \\  & =9-3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=2,$ the velocity is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =9-3(2)^{2} \\  & =9-12 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed is $|-3|=3\,\text{mm/s}.$

questions.problem: A website receives $v(h)$ visits every $h$ hours. What are the units of $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}h}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We have that the time $h$ is measured in hours and the number of visits is measured in visitors. 

$$
\begin{aligned}h: & \text{hours} \\ v(h): & \text{visitors}\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}h}$ measures a change in $v$ over a change in $h.$ So, it represents a ratio of the units:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}h}: & \frac{\text{visitors}}{\text{hours}}\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}h}$ is measured in "visitors per hour ".

**Step 1:** First, we write the inverse function implicitly. The given function is $y={3}^{2x+4},$ and to write the inverse function implicitly, we swap $x$ and $y$ as follows:

$$
x={3}^{2y+4}
$$

Note that in the equation above, we have $y={h}^{-1}(x).$

**Step 2:** Next, we differentiate. The overall goal is to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ but the equation is already solved for $x,$ so we compute $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}$ and then take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({3}^{2y+4}) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & ={3}^{2y+4}\cdot \operatorname{ln}3\cdot 2 \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & ={3}^{2(y+2)}\cdot \operatorname{ln}({3}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & ={9}^{y+2}\operatorname{ln}9 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{9}^{y+2}\operatorname{ln}9} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{9}^{-y}}{81\operatorname{ln}9}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Lastly, we write the result in terms of ${h}^{-1}(x).$ Since $y={h}^{-1}(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{h}^{-1}(x)] & =\frac{{9}^{-{h}^{-1}(x)}}{81\operatorname{ln}9} \\ {({h}^{-1})}^{'}(x) & =\frac{{9}^{-{h}^{-1}(x)}}{81\operatorname{ln}9}.\end{aligned}
$$

y>-2x+1,

$$
2x+y>1.
$$

Now consider the line $y=x.$ Since the line is dashed, the inequality is strict. Also, since the shaded region lies  *below* the line, the inequality is a "less than"  inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y<x.
$$

Therefore, the system of inequalities that defines the shaded region is

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x+y>1 \\ y<x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The geometric series $1+5+25+125+625$ can be written using sigma notation as
questions.worked_solution:

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{N}{a}_{1}{r}^{n-1},
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ denotes the first term of the series, $r$ denotes the common ratio, and $N$ denotes the number of terms in the series. In this case, ${a}_{1}=1$ and $N=5.$

To find $r,$ we calculate the ratio of the first two terms in the series:

$$

$$

Therefore, expressing the geometric series given in sigma notation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}1+5+25+125+625 & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}1\cdot {5}^{n-1} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{5}{5}^{n-1}.\end{aligned}

Now we must determine $N$ (the index of the last term). To do this, we use the fact that

$$
{a}_{N}={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{N-1}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{N} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{N-1} \\ 7 & =2\,401\cdot {(\frac{1}{7})}^{N-1} \\ \frac{7}{2\,401} & ={(\frac{1}{7})}^{N-1} \\ \frac{1}{343} & =\frac{1}{{7}^{N-1}} \\ 343 & ={7}^{N-1} \\ {7}^{3} & ={7}^{N-1} \\ 3 & =N-1 \\ N & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing the geometric series in sigma notation, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\,401+343+⋯+7 & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{4}2\,401\cdot {(\frac{1}{7})}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=4,$ we have

From the table, we obtain ${f}^{-1}(4)=1$ and ${f}^{'}(1)=-2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{'}(4) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(4))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{7}\frac{1}{9}(5)^{n-1}.$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=3x+\sqrt{x}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ 3x+\sqrt{x} & =2 \\ \sqrt{x} & =2-3x \\ x & =4-12x+9{x}^{2} \\ 9{x}^{2}-13x+4 & =0 \\ (9x-4)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =\frac{4}{9},\,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Checking the solutions, we notice that only $x=\frac{4}{9}$ satisfies the equation $3x+\sqrt{x}=2.$ Therefore, we discard $x=1$ and conclude that ${f}^{-1}(2)=\frac{4}{9}.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3x+\sqrt{x} \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =3+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9}) & =3+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{(\frac{4}{9})}} \\ {f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9}) & =3+\frac{3}{4} \\ {f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9}) & =\frac{15}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9})} \\  & =\frac{4}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the geometric series ${\sum }_{n=0}^{4}2{(3)}^{n-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the given series is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n-1},$ it is a geometric series. Notice that the index starts from $n=0$ instead of $n=1.$

To determine the sum, we use the formula for the sum ${S}_{N}$ of a geometric series.

$$
{S}_{N}={a}_{0}\frac{(1-{r}^{N})}{1-r}
$$

In this case, $r=3.$ Also, note that $N=5,$ since there are $5$ terms in total.

The formula for the $n$th term of the series is

$$
{a}_{n}=2{(3)}^{n-1},
$$

and so the first term ${a}_{0}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{0} & =2{(3)}^{0-1} \\  & =2{(3)}^{-1} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we substitute ${a}_{0}=\frac{2}{3},r=3$ and $N=5$ into the formula for ${S}_{N}$, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{5} & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{(1-{3}^{5})}{(1-3)} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{(1-{3}^{5})}{(-2)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-242) \\  & =\frac{242}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base.

To do this, we write $81$ as ${3}^{4},$ and then we rewrite the right-hand side using the power rule of exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{81}^{2a} & =\frac{1}{{3}^{a-1}} \\ {({3}^{4})}^{2a} & =\frac{1}{{3}^{a-1}} \\ {3}^{8a} & =\frac{1}{{3}^{a-1}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using a negative exponent: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{8a} & ={3}^{-(a-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(3),$ we equate the exponents and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}8a & =-(a-1) \\ 8a & =-a+1 \\ 9a & =1 \\ a & =\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find ${f}^{'}(x)$  for $f(x)=\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}2x}{9}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of arcsine is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsin}x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}.
$$

Using the chain rule and the formula above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}2x}{9}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcsin}2x) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(2x)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{9\sqrt{1-4{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}(2x) & =0 \\ {10}^{\operatorname{log}(2x)} & ={10}^{0}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${10}^{\operatorname{log}(2x)}=2x.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={10}^{0} \\ 2x & =1 \\ x & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}(x-2) & ={log}_{2}(2x-3) \\ x-2 & =2x-3 \\ -x & =-1 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation: 

- Substituting $x=1$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}(x-2) & \overset{?}{=}{log}_{2}(2x-3) \\ {log}_{2}(1-2) & \overset{?}{=}{log}_{2}(2\cdot 1-3) \\ {log}_{2}(-1) & \overset{?}{=}{log}_{2}(-1)\end{aligned}
