questions.problem: Factor the expression ${r}^{4}-(5s)^{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The difference of squares formula is given by

$$
{a}^{2}-{b}^{2}=(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Notice that our expression can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
{r}^{4}-(5s)^{4}={({r}^{2})}^{2}-{((5s)^{2})}^{2}
$$

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{({r}^{2})}^{2}-{((5s)^{2})}^{2} & =({r}^{2}+(5s)^{2})({r}^{2}-(5s)^{2}) \\  & =({r}^{2}+25{s}^{2})({r}^{2}-(5s)^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we notice that the expression in the second set of parentheses is also a difference of squares. Therefore, the expression can be factored further, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}({r}^{2}+25{s}^{2})({r}^{2}-(5s)^{2}) & =({r}^{2}+25{s}^{2})(r+5s)(r-5s)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Joseph is measuring the height reached by his lime tree by recording the following two numbers for different values of $t,$ where $t$ is the time, in years, since he planted the tree:

- $H(t)$ - The tree's height, in centimeters

- $r(t)$ - the rate at which the tree's height is increasing.

What is the relationship between $H(t)$ and $r(t)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The function $H(t)$ gives the tree's height after $t$ years. Then,

$$
{H}^{'}(t)=\frac{\text{d}H(t)}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{Change in }H}{\text{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, ${H}^{'}(t)$ gives the rate at which the height of the tree increases at time $t$, which is the same as $r(t).$ Therefore, the relationship between $H(t)$ and $r(t)$ is ${H}^{'}(t)=r(t).$

questions.problem: The budget of a school varies over the year. The budget $B,$ in thousands of dollars, after $t$ months since the beginning of the school can be modeled by the function $B(t)=(t-1)^{2}{e}^{-t}+10$ thousands of dollars. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the budget as a function of $t?$
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the budget is equal to ${B}^{'}(t).$ 

We take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{'}(t) & =2(t-1){e}^{-t}-(t-1)^{2}{e}^{-t} \\  & ={e}^{-t}(2t-2-{t}^{2}+2t-1) \\  & ={e}^{-t}(4t-3-{t}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the school budget is ${e}^{-t}(4t-3-{t}^{2})$ thousands of dollars per month.

questions.problem: What is the multiplicity of the root $x=4$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+32?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=4$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-4)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $4$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $0$ | $32$ |
|  | $↓$ | $4$ | $-8$ | $-32$ |
|  | $1$ | $-2$ | $-8$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-4}={x}^{2}-2x-8,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-4)({x}^{2}-2x-8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-4)(x+2)(x-4) \\  & =(x+2)(x-4)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-4)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=4$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.problem: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x)=5{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}$ have multiplicity $2?$

$$

$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $x$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

- The factor $(x-3)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=3$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $10,$ and the leading coefficient is $8.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }10}{\text{factor of }8}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $-\frac{5}{4}=\frac{-5}{4}$ takes the above form since the numerator $(-5)$ is a factor of $10$ and the denominator $(4)$ is a factor of $8.$

questions.problem: Find the roots of $f(w)=\frac{{w}^{2}-3w-10}{2{w}^{2}-10w}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(w)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(w)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{w}^{2}-3w-10}{2{w}^{2}-10w}=0.
$$

First, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(w) & =\frac{{w}^{2}-3w-10}{2{w}^{2}-10w} \\  & =\frac{(w+2)(w-5)}{2w(w-5)} \\  & =\frac{(w+2)\cancel{(w-5)}}{2w\cancel{(w-5)}} \\  & =\frac{(w+2)}{2w}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $w:$

$$
\begin{aligned}w+2 & =0\,⟹\,w=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to $f(w)=0$ is $w=-2.$

questions.problem: What are the solutions of the equation $6{y}^{2}+14=0?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{2}+14 & =0 \\ 6{y}^{2} & =-14 \\ {y}^{2} & =-\frac{14}{6} \\ {y}^{2} & =-\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

By taking square root, we obtain:

$$
y=\pm \sqrt{-\frac{7}{3}}
$$

We now rewrite $y$ using the imaginary unit $\text{i}=\sqrt{-1}\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \sqrt{-\frac{7}{3}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{7}{3}\cdot (-1)} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{3}}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{3}}\text{i} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{21}}{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify $\frac{2w-5}{5w}+\frac{w+7}{5w}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We have a common denominator of $5w,$ so we add the numerators and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2w-5}{5w}+\frac{w+7}{5w} & = \\ \frac{2w-5+w+7}{5w} & = \\ \frac{(2w+w)+(-5+7)}{5w} & = \\ \frac{3w+2}{5w} & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $\frac{3}{2z}=p$ and $\frac{2}{z}=q,$ what is $p-q?$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to subtract the following fractions:

$$
p-q=\frac{3}{2z}-\frac{2}{z}
$$

In order to subtract the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. Here, we can put both fractions over a common denominator of $2z$ if we multiply the top and bottom of the second fraction by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2z}-\frac{2}{z} & = \\ \frac{3}{2z}-\frac{2}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{z} & = \\ \frac{3}{2z}-\frac{4}{2z} & = \\ \frac{3-4}{2z} & = \\ -\frac{1}{2z} & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $\frac{7}{5d}=g$ and $\frac{2f}{d}=h,$ what is $g-h?$
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to subtract the following fractions:

$$
g-h=\frac{7}{5d}-\frac{2f}{d}
$$

In order to subtract the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. Here, we can put both fractions over a common denominator of $5d$ if we multiply the top and bottom of the second fraction by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{5d}-\frac{2f}{d} & = \\ \frac{7}{5d}-\frac{5}{5}\cdot \frac{2f}{d} & = \\ \frac{7}{5d}-\frac{10f}{5d} & = \\ \frac{7-10f}{5d} & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify $\frac{3w}{v(2+w)}-\frac{5}{4v(2+w)}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In order to subtract the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. Here, we can put both fractions over a common denominator of $4v(1+w)$ if we multiply the top and bottom of the first fraction by $4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3w}{v(2+w)}-\frac{5}{4v(2+w)} & = \\ \frac{4}{4}\cdot \frac{3w}{v(2+w)}-\frac{5}{4v(2+w)} & = \\ \frac{12w}{4v(2+w)}-\frac{5}{4v(2+w)} & = \\ \frac{12w-5}{4v(2+w)} & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify $\frac{t}{(t-3)(u+4)}+\frac{5}{u+4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In order to add the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. Here, we can put both fractions over a common denominator of $(t-3)(u+4)$ if we multiply the top and bottom of the second fraction by $t-3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{t}{(t-3)(u+4)}+\frac{5}{u+4} & = \\ \frac{t}{(t-3)(u+4)}+\frac{t-3}{t-3}\cdot \frac{5}{u+4} & = \\ \frac{t}{(t-3)(u+4)}+\frac{5(t-3)}{(t-3)(u+4)} & = \\ \frac{t+5(t-3)}{(t-3)(u+4)} & = \\ \frac{t+5t-15}{(t-3)(u+4)} & = \\ \frac{6t-15}{(t-3)(u+4)} & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify $\frac{5m}{n(m-4)}+\frac{n}{m-4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In order to add the two fractions, we need them to have a common denominator. Here, we can put both fractions over a common denominator of $n(m-4)$ if we multiply the top and bottom of the second fraction by $n:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5m}{n(m-4)}+\frac{n}{m-4} & = \\ \frac{5m}{n(m-4)}+\frac{n}{n}\cdot \frac{n}{m-4} & = \\ \frac{5m}{n(m-4)}+\frac{n\cdot n}{n(m-4)} & = \\ \frac{5m}{n(m-4)}+\frac{{n}^{2}}{n(m-4)} & = \\ \frac{5m+{n}^{2}}{n(m-4)} & \end{aligned}
$$

The graph represents the function $y=\frac{a}{x-b}+k.$ What is the value of $a+b+k?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the horizontal asymptote of the graph is $y=2,$ while the vertical asymptote is $x=1.$ This means that $k=2$ and $b=1,$ and we can re-write our function as

$$
y=\frac{a}{x-1}+2.
$$

Also, we are given that the point $(2,5)$ lies on the graph. Substituting its coordinates into the equation above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{a}{x-1}+2 \\ 5 & =\frac{a}{2-1}+2 \\ 3 & =\frac{a}{1} \\ a & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a+b+k=3+1+2=6.$

questions.problem: Calculate the vertical asymptotes of $f(x)=\frac{2x+4}{{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+3x-3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2x+4}{{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+3x-3} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2)}{{x}^{2}(x-1)+3(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{2(x+2)}{({x}^{2}+3)(x-1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives

$$
({x}^{2}+3)(x-1)=0.
$$

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

- Solving $x-1=0$ gives the solution $x=1.$

- The equation ${x}^{2}+3=0$ has no real solutions.

Therefore, the only vertical asymptote is $x=1.$

questions.problem: Find all of the vertical asymptotes of the function $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+x+1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+1}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+x+1} \\  & =\frac{x+1}{{x}^{2}(x+1)+(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{x+1}{(x+1)({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x+1}}{\cancel{(x+1)}({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+1=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, $f(x)$ does not have any vertical asymptotes.

questions.problem: Determine the vertical asymptotes of the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}-3x}{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+x-3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-3x}{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+x-3} \\  & =\frac{x(x-3)}{{x}^{2}(x-3)+(x-3)} \\  & =\frac{x(x-3)}{(x-3)({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{x\cancel{(x-3)}}{\cancel{(x-3)}({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+1=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

questions.problem: Calculate $\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=20$, and we get

$$
\int {x}^{20}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{20+1}}{20+1}+C=\frac{{x}^{21}}{21}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{21}}{21}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{21}}{21})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{21}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{21})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{21}\cdot 21{x}^{20} & = \\ {x}^{20}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $F(x)$ given that $f(x)={x}^{17}$ and ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=17$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{17}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{17+1}}{17+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{18}}{18}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{18}}{18}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{18}}{18})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{18}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{18})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{18}\cdot 18\,{x}^{17} & = \\ {x}^{17}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the antiderivative of ${x}^{1/4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{4}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{1/4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{1/4+1}}{(\frac{1}{4}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5/4}}{(\frac{5}{4})}+C \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{5/4}}{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4{x}^{5/4}}{5}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4{x}^{5/4}}{5})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{4}{5}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{5/4})+0 & = \\ \frac{4}{5}\cdot \frac{5}{4}{x}^{5/4-1} & = \\ {x}^{1/4}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate the integral of $\sqrt[5]{{x}^{3}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt[5]{{x}^{3}}={x}^{3/5}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{3}{5}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt[5]{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{3/5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3/5+1}}{(\frac{3}{5}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8/5}}{(\frac{8}{5})}+C \\  & =\frac{5{x}^{8/5}}{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5{x}^{8/5}}{8}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5{x}^{8/5}}{8})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{5}{8}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{8/5})+0 & = \\ \frac{5}{8}\cdot \frac{8}{5}{x}^{8/5-1} & = \\ {x}^{3/5}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the antiderivative of $\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by writing the root as a rational power, $\sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}={x}^{2/5}.$ So, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{2}{5}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt[5]{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{2/5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2/5+1}}{(\frac{2}{5}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{7/5}}{(\frac{7}{5})}+C \\  & =\frac{5{x}^{7/5}}{7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5{x}^{7/5}}{7}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5{x}^{7/5}}{7})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{5}{7}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7/5})+0 & = \\ \frac{5}{7}\cdot \frac{7}{5}{x}^{7/5-1} & = \\ {x}^{2/5}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{4/3}}$ and that ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{4/3}}={x}^{-4/3}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{4}{3}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-4/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-4/3+1}}{(-\frac{4}{3}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-1/3}}{(-\frac{1}{3})}+C \\  & =-3{x}^{-1/3}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{{x}^{1/3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{3{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{3{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{-6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\frac{{x}^{-6+1}}{-6+1})+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\frac{{x}^{-5}}{-5})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{15}\cdot {x}^{-5}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{15{x}^{5}}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{3}{2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{2{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{3}{2}\int {y}^{-2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot (\frac{{y}^{(-2+1)}}{-2+1})+C \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot (\frac{{y}^{-1}}{-1})+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\cdot {y}^{-1}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{2y}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{5}{{x}^{11}}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{{x}^{11}}\,\text{d}x & =5\int {x}^{-11}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\cdot (\frac{{x}^{-11+1}}{-11+1})+C \\  & =5\cdot (\frac{{x}^{-10}}{-10})+C \\  & =-\frac{5}{10}\cdot {x}^{-10}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2{x}^{10}}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{5}\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{5}\int {x}^{0}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{5}\cdot \frac{{x}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & =\sqrt{5}\cdot x+C \\  & =\sqrt{5}x+C\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we can see that for any constant $k,$ we have $\int k\,\text{d}x=kx+C.$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int {e}^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={e}^{2}\int 1\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2}\int {x}^{0}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{2}\cdot \frac{{x}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & ={e}^{2}\cdot x+C \\  & ={e}^{2}x+C\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we can see that for any constant $k,$ we have $\int k\,\text{d}x=kx+C.$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int (-5)\,\text{d}y.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can just take the constant factor out of the integral, and then apply the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-5)\,\text{d}y & =-5\int 1\,\text{d}y \\  & =-5\int {y}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-5\cdot \frac{{y}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & =-5\cdot y+C \\  & =-5y+C\end{aligned}
$$

In general, we can see that for any constant $k,$ we have $\int k\,\text{d}x=kx+C.$

questions.problem: Find the antiderivative of $\sqrt[4]{x}-{x}^{5}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the sum rule, we compute the sum of the integrals of each function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt[4]{x}-{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{1/4}\,\text{d}x-\int {x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{1/4+1}}{(\frac{1}{4}+1)}-\frac{{x}^{5+1}}{(5+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{5/4}}{(\frac{5}{4})}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{(6)}+C \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt[4]{{x}^{5}}}{5}-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the result of dividing $\frac{3}{5{z}^{2}}$ by $\frac{4}{{z}^{5}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute

$$
\frac{3}{5{z}^{2}}÷\frac{4}{{z}^{5}},
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5{z}^{2}}÷\frac{4}{{z}^{5}} & = \\ \frac{3}{5{z}^{2}}\cdot \frac{{z}^{5}}{4} & = \\ \frac{3{z}^{5}}{20{z}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{3{z}^{3}\cdot {z}^{2}}{20{z}^{2}} & = \\ \frac{3{z}^{3}\cdot \cancel{{z}^{2}}}{20\cancel{{z}^{2}}} & = \\ \frac{3{z}^{3}}{20} & \end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the final step, we canceled out a common factor of ${z}^{2}$ in the numerator and denominator.

questions.problem: $\frac{3rs}{7t}÷\frac{r}{7st}=$

\frac{3rs}{7t}÷\frac{r}{7st},
$$

we just need to multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3rs}{7t}÷\frac{r}{7st} & = \\ \frac{3rs}{7t}\cdot \frac{7st}{r} & = \\ \frac{3s\cdot r}{7t}\cdot \frac{7t\cdot s}{r} & = \\ \frac{3s\cdot \cancel{r}}{\cancel{7t}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{7t}\cdot s}{\cancel{r}} & = \\ 3{s}^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{5}\sqrt{x-1}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

 

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}\sqrt{x-1}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{x-1},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}\sqrt{x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\sqrt{1+\frac{4i}{n}-1}\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\sqrt{\frac{4i}{n}}\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\sqrt{\frac{i}{n}}\cdot \frac{8}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int (3\operatorname{cos}x-2\operatorname{sec}x\,\operatorname{tan}x)\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$

questions.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={e}^{x},$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-0}{n}=\frac{2}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(0+k\cdot \frac{2}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(\frac{2k}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[{e}^{2k/n}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the roots of the polynomial $p(m)=12{m}^{3}-40{m}^{2}+32m.$

$$

First, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $4m.$ We can factor out the $4m$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4m(3{m}^{2}-10m+8) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $3{m}^{2}-10m+8$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4m(3{m}^{2}-10m+8) & =0 \\ 4m(3m-4)(m-2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the zero product rule, the solutions are $m=0,$ $m=\frac{4}{3},$ and $m=2.$

$$

Next, notice that all of the terms of the polynomial have a common factor of $4{h}^{3}.$ We can factor out the $4{h}^{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{h}^{5}-32{h}^{4}-20{h}^{3} & =0 \\ 4{h}^{3}(4{h}^{2}-8h-5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the expression $4{h}^{2}-8h-5$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{h}^{3}(4{h}^{2}-8h-5) & =0 \\ 4{h}^{3}(2h+1)(2h-5) & =0\end{aligned}

$$

Then, we solve $(m-3)({m}^{2}-2)=0$ by setting each factor equal to $0.$

- Setting the factor $(m-3)$ equal to $0,$ we get

$$

$$

Therefore, the solutions are $m=3,\,\pm \sqrt{2}.$

Finally, we set each factor equal to $0$ and solve:

questions.problem:
Which of the following equations have no real solution?

I. - $\sqrt{7x+4}=-9$
II. - $\sqrt{3x-2}=3$
III. - $\sqrt{9x-5}=-2$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that a square root is always positive or zero. So, a radical equation has no real solution if it states that a square root is equal to a negative number.

Of the given equations, only I and III state that a square is equal to a negative number. Therefore, equations I and III have no real solution.

So, the correct answer is "I and III only".

First, let's simplify the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & \ge 27-2{x}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+2{x}^{2} & \ge 27 \\ 3{x}^{2} & \ge 27 \\ {x}^{2} & \ge 9\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use either of two methods to solve the inequality.

*Method 1 - Solving an Absolute Value Equation*

Taking the square root of both sides of the inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & \ge 9 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & \ge \sqrt{9} \\ |x| & \ge 3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the definition of absolute value, we must have 

$$
x\le -3\,\text{or}\,x\ge 3.
$$

So, the solution is $\,x\in (-\infty ,-3]\cup [3,\infty ).$

*Method 2 - Picturing a Quadratic Curve*

Starting from ${x}^{2}\ge 9$ and moving all terms to the left-hand side, we reach

$$
{x}^{2}-9\ge 0.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding parabola given by $y={x}^{2}-9$ and find its roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =9 \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{9} \\  & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

So the roots are $x=\pm 3.$ 

Since the leading coefficient of ${x}^{2}-9$ is positive, the parabola opens upward. Therefore, the solution to the given inequality ($y\ge 0$) lies outside the roots (and include them).

![](images/f2/f277a8b22194fae2d932f6f39ac28e869955486820c195f5e027a9bc49cd493c.png)

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (-\infty ,-3]\cup [3,\infty ).$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the downward-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(2,4)$ and which passes through the point $(4,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
For any upward or downward-opening parabola with its vertex at $(h,k),$ the general standard equation is given by

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k).
$$

Here, the vertex has coordinates $(h,k)=(2,4).$ Substituting these into the general standard equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =4p(y-4).\end{aligned}
$$

We are left to find the value of $p.$ We know that the given parabola also passes through the point $(4,1),$ so we can substitute $x=4$ and $y=1$ into the standard equation and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =4p(y-4) \\ (4-2)^{2} & =4p(1-4) \\ 4 & =-12p \\ p & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2} & =4p(y-4) \\ (x-2)^{2} & =4(-\frac{1}{3})(y-4) \\ (x-2)^{2} & =-\frac{4}{3}(y-4).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{ln}^{2}x}{x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{ln}^{2}x=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to \infty }x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{ln}^{2}x}{x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[{ln}^{2}x]^{'}}{{[x]}^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}x}{x})}{1} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{2\operatorname{ln}x}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\operatorname{ln}x)^{2}}{x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{2\operatorname{ln}x}{x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[2\operatorname{ln}x]^{'}}{[x]^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2}{x})}{1} \\  & =2{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{x} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{cos}x)}{\operatorname{tan}x} & ={lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{[\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{cos}x)]^{'}}{{[\operatorname{tan}x]}^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x})}{{sec}^{2}x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{\operatorname{cos}x})}{(\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}x})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{sin}x{cos}^{2}x}{\operatorname{cos}x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {\frac{\pi }{2}}^{-}}\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cot}2x}{\operatorname{cot}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}2x=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\operatorname{cot}x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{\operatorname{cot}2x}{\operatorname{cot}x} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{[\operatorname{cot}2x]^{'}}{[\operatorname{cot}x]^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{(-2{csc}^{2}2x)}{-{csc}^{2}x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{2\cdot (\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}2x})}{(\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{2{sin}^{2}x}{{sin}^{2}2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{2{sin}^{2}x}{{(2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x)}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{2{sin}^{2}x}{4{sin}^{2}x{cos}^{2}x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{2\cancel{{sin}^{2}x}}{4\cancel{{sin}^{2}x}{cos}^{2}x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{2{cos}^{2}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{cos}^{2}0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the solution of $\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-x\le x+\frac{5}{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the given inequality so that the right-hand side equals zero. Then, we factor the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-x & \le x+\frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-2x-\frac{5}{2} & \le 0 \\ \frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-4x-5) & \le 0 \\ \frac{1}{2}(x+1)(x-5) & \le 0 \\ (x+1)(x-5) & \le 0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the roots of the corresponding equation $(x+1)(x-5)=0.$ The roots are $x=-1$ and $x=5,$ and they split the number line into $3$ subintervals $(-\infty ,-1),$ $(-1,5)$ and $(5,\infty ).$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $(-1,5)$ | $(5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x+1$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $(x+1)(x-5)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

Finally, to solve the quadratic inequality $(x+1)(x-5)\le 0,$ we look at the bottom row to find out where the expression $(x+1)(x-5)$ is zero or negative.

We see that the expression is negative on the interval $(-1,5).$ Also, we know that the expression equals $0$ at the points $x=-1$ and $x=5.$

Therefore, we conclude that $\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-x\le x+\frac{5}{2}$ for all $x\in [-1,5].$

questions.problem: Find the solution of $\frac{1}{10}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{10}x\le 2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the given inequality so that the right-hand side equals zero. Then, we factor the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{10}x & \le 2 \\ \frac{1}{10}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{10}x-2 & \le 0 \\ \frac{1}{10}({x}^{2}+x-20) & \le 0 \\ \frac{1}{10}(x+5)(x-4) & \le 0 \\ (x+5)(x-4) & \le 0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the roots of the corresponding equation $(x+5)(x-4)=0.$ The roots are $x=-5$ and $x=4,$ and they split the number line into $3$ subintervals $(-\infty ,-5),$ $(-5,4)$ and $(4,\infty ).$

Now, we construct a sign table with the list of the intervals on the top and the list of factors on the left. Filling in the sign table using the usual method, we get the following result:

|  | $(-\infty ,-5)$ | $(-5,4)$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x+5$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $x-4$ | $-$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| $(x+5)(x-4)$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

Finally, to solve the quadratic inequality $(x+5)(x-4)\le 0,$ we look at the bottom row to find out where the expression $(x+5)(x-4)$ is zero or negative.

We see that the expression is negative on the interval $(-5,4).$ Also, we know that the expression equals $0$ at the points $x=-5$ and $x=4.$

Therefore, we conclude that $\frac{1}{10}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{10}x\le 2$ for all $x\in [-5,4].$

questions.problem: The area under the curve $y=(x+1)^{3}$ between $x=0$ and $x=4$ and the $x$-axis is approximated by a right Riemann sum using $n$ subintervals of equal length. What is the expression for the Riemann sum in sigma notation?
questions.worked_solution:
The right Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}f({x}_{j})Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx$ with $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

We're told that there are $n$ subintervals. The endpoints indicate that $a=0$ and $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-0}{n}=\frac{4}{n}.
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the right Riemann sum can be expressed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}f({x}_{j})Δx & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}f(a+jΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[f(0+j\cdot \frac{4}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[f(\frac{4j}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[\frac{4}{n}{(\frac{4j}{n}+1)}^{3}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](images/63/63fe9cf3a61a5cef09f9c19e16a18318338faa6837eeb77b83f49b636157bb95.png)

A sphere is decreasing in volume at a rate of $54\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ Calculate the rate at which the radius of the sphere is decreasing at the moment when the radius is $3\,\text{cm}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-54\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=3\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-54\pi $ and $r=3,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-54\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (3)^{2} \\ -54\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 36\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the sphere is decreasing at a rate of $1.5\text{ cm/s}$ when the radius is $3\,\text{cm}.$

questions.worked_solution:
In order for a point $(a,b)$ to lie on the graph of the function $y=\operatorname{arcsin}x,$ the following conditions must hold:

- The reflected point $(b,a)$ must lie on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}x,$ meaning $a=\operatorname{sin}b.$

- The $y$-value of the point must lie in the range of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}x,$ which is $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}].$

With this in mind, let's check each of the points. 

- First, we consider the point $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\pi }{4}).$ We note the following:

- The point $(-\frac{\pi }{4},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$  lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}x.\,✓$

- The range of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}x$ is $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ and $y=-\frac{\pi }{4}$ lies within this range. $\,✓$

Therefore, the point $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\pi }{4})$ lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}x.$

- Next, we consider the point $(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{5\pi }{3}).$ We note the following:

- The point $(\frac{5\pi }{3},-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})$ lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}x.\,✓$

- The range of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}x$ is $y\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ and $y=\frac{5\pi }{3}$ does **not** lie within this range. $\,\times $

Therefore, the point $(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{5\pi }{3})$ does **not** lie on the graph of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}x.$

- Finally, we consider the point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\pi }{4}).$ We note the following:

- The point $(\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})$ does **not** lie on the graph of $y=\operatorname{sin}x.$ $\,\times $

Therefore, the point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\pi }{4})$ does **not** lie on the graph of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following systems is a first-order initial value problem?

I. - $(1+{x}^{2}){y}^{'}=8y,\,y(-1)=3$
II. - $8{y}^{'}-xy=3$
III. - $3{y}^{''}=4y,\,y(-1)=0,\,{y}^{'}(-1)=1$
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order initial value problem (or IVP) is a first-order ordinary differential equation together with an initial condition that specifies a value of the unknown function at a point in its domain. A first-order initial value problem typically takes the form

$$
{y}^{'}=f(x,y),\,y({x}_{0})={y}_{0},
$$

where ${x}_{0}$ and ${y}_{0}$ are constants.

With that in mind, let's check each option.

- System I is a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a first-order differential equation $(1+{x}^{2}){y}^{'}=8y$ together with the initial condition $y(-1)=3.$

- System II is not a first-order initial value problem. We have a first-order ordinary differential equation, but there is no initial condition.

- System III is not a first-order initial value problem. It consists of a *second*-order differential equation $3{y}^{''}=4y$ together with *two* initial conditions $y(-1)=0,\,{y}^{'}(-1)=1.$ This is a second-order initial value problem.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem: What is the distance between the points $A(8,-3,-1)$ and $B(12,5,-2)?$

Which of the following are autonomous ordinary differential equations?

I. - ${y}^{'}-8{e}^{y}=2$
II. - $y{y}^{'}+3=\operatorname{cos}y$
III. - $x{y}^{'}-8={e}^{y}$
questions.worked_solution:
An ordinary differential equation with dependent variable $y$ and independent variable $x$ is said to be autonomous if it can be written in the form $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y),$ or equivalently, ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

With that in mind, let's check each of the differential equations:

- Equation I is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form ${y}^{'}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'}-8{e}^{y} & =2 \\ {y}^{'} & =8{e}^{y}+2 \\ {y}^{'} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=8{e}^{y}+2.$

- Equation II is an autonomous differential equation. Writing the equation in the form ${y}^{'}=f(y),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y{y}^{'}+3 & =\operatorname{cos}y \\ {y}^{'} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}y-3}{y} \\ {y}^{'} & =f(y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}y-3}{y}.$

- Equation III is not an autonomous differential equation. If we isolate the derivative term, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{'}-8 & ={e}^{y} \\ {y}^{'} & =\frac{{e}^{y}+8}{x} \\ {y}^{'} & =f(x,y)\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{y}+8}{x}.$ So, it is not possible to write the equation in the form ${y}^{'}=f(y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem: A pedestal for a statue consists of eight identical stone blocks in the form of a rectangular solid. Each block is $20\,\text{ft}$ long, $15\,\text{ft}$ wide, and $2\,\text{ft}$ high. What is the total combined volume of the pedestal?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the volume of one block.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=20,\,w=15,\,h=2
$$

into the formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}V=20\cdot 15\cdot 2=600\,{\text{ft}}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total volume of the eight blocks is

$$
600\cdot 8=4\,800\,{\text{ft}}^{3}.
$$

questions.problem: Simplify the expression $\operatorname{sec}\theta +\frac{\operatorname{tan}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's interpret the fraction as a division:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{tan}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }=\operatorname{tan}\theta ÷\operatorname{sin}\theta 
$$

Then, we recall the identity $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ and we substitute it into the above expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}\theta ÷\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =(\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta })÷\operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we turn the division into multiplication, and simplify the expression as much as possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}\theta +(\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta })÷\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =\operatorname{sec}\theta +\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{sec}\theta +\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot 1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{sec}\theta +\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{sec}\theta +\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}\theta }}{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \cancel{\operatorname{sin}\theta }} \\  & =\operatorname{sec}\theta +\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{sec}\theta +\operatorname{sec}\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sec}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sec}\theta +\frac{\operatorname{tan}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }=2\operatorname{sec}\theta .$

questions.problem: Simplify the expression $\operatorname{tan}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{csc}\theta .$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the identities $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }$ and $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ and we substitute them into the given expression:

$$
\operatorname{tan}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta }
$$

Now, we multiply the three quantities:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta } \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta }}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta }} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{tan}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{csc}\theta =1.$

questions.problem: Given that  $7\operatorname{sin}\theta =17\operatorname{cos}\theta ,$ calculate $\operatorname{tan}\theta .$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the identity $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }.$

To write the equation in terms of $\operatorname{tan}\theta $ only, we divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}\theta ,$ and apply the above identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =17\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 7\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta } & =17\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\ 7\operatorname{tan}\theta  & =17\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we isolate $\operatorname{tan}\theta $ by dividing both sides of the equation by $7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7\operatorname{tan}\theta }{7} & =\frac{17}{7} \\ \operatorname{tan}\theta  & =\frac{17}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify the trigonometric expression $\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's interpret the fraction as a division:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}=(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta )÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1)
$$

Then, we recall the identities $\operatorname{cot}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }$ and $\operatorname{sec}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ and we substitute them into the above expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta )÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta )÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify, turn the division into multiplication, and then simplify again:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta )÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta })÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \cancel{\operatorname{sin}\theta }}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \cancel{\operatorname{sin}\theta }})÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1)÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1)\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}=1.$

questions.problem:
Find the exact value of $\operatorname{cos}(-{75}^{∘}).$

*Hint: Use the fact that $-{75}^{∘}={60}^{∘}-{135}^{∘}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the difference formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}(x-y)=\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{cos}y+\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{sin}y
$$

Applying the difference formula for cosine with $x={60}^{∘}$ and $y={135}^{∘},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(-{75}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{cos}({60}^{∘}-{135}^{∘}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}{60}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}{135}^{∘}+\operatorname{sin}{60}^{∘}\operatorname{sin}{135}^{∘} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}+\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Of $12$ people attending a seminar, $4$ participants have black hair, and the rest have brown hair. Define $A$ to be the event "a participant has black hair." What is ${A}^{'}$ described in natural language, and what is $P({A}^{'})?$
questions.worked_solution:
The **complement** of an event $A,$ denoted ${A}^{'},$ is the *opposite* of $A.$ That is to say, ${A}^{'}$  is the set of outcomes in which $A$ *does not* happen.

Here, ${A}^{'}$ is the opposite of the event "a participant has black hair." So ${A}^{'}$ is the event "a participant doesn't have black hair." In other words, the event ${A}^{'}$ is "a participant has brown hair."

Now, let's calculate the probability $P({A}^{'}).$ The sample space is 

$$
S={\text{black hair, brown hair}},
$$

and since there is a different number of participants with of each hair color, we have different probabilities of a participant having "black hair" or "brown hair."

Of $12$ people, $8$ of them have brown hair. Therefore, 

$$
P({A}^{'})=\frac{8}{12}=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

questions.problem: Mary owns $5$ orange shirts, and $15$ shirts in other colors. Define $A$ to be the event "Mary wears an orange shirt." What is ${A}^{'}$ described in natural language, and what is $P({A}^{'})?$
questions.worked_solution:
The **complement** of an event $A,$ denoted ${A}^{'},$ is the *opposite* of $A.$ That is to say, ${A}^{'}$  is the set of outcomes in which $A$ *does not* happen.

Here, ${A}^{'}$ is the opposite of the event "Mary wears an orange shirt." So ${A}^{'}$ is the event "Mary doesn't wear an orange shirt." In other words, the event ${A}^{'}$ is "Mary wears a non-orange shirt."

Now, let's calculate the probability $P({A}^{'}).$ The sample space is 

$$
S={\text{orange shirt, non-orange shirt}},
$$

and since there is a different number of shirts of each color, we have different probabilities of having an "orange" or "non-orange" shirt.

Mary owns $20$ shirts, and $15$ of them are non-orange. Therefore,

$$
P({A}^{'})=\frac{15}{20}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

questions.problem:
Two fair $6$-sided dice are rolled. Define $A$ to be the event "the sum of outcomes is a prime number" Which of the following statements are true regarding this event?

I. - $P(A)=0.42$ to $2$ decimal places
II. - ${A}^{'}$ is the event "the sum of the outcomes is an even number"
III. - $P({A}^{'})=0.58$ to $2$ decimal places
questions.worked_solution:
Let's inspect each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. There are $36$ possible outcomes and $15$ of these have the sum of the outcomes equal to a prime, namely 

$$
\begin{aligned} & (1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(1,4),(4,1),(2,3),(3,2),(1,6), \\  & (6,1),(3,4),(4,3),(2,5),(5,2),(5,6),(6,5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(A)=\frac{15}{36}=0.42
$$

to $2$ decimal places.

- Statement II is false. The complement of $A$ is the event ${A}^{'},$ "the sum of the outcomes is a composite number".

- Statement III is true. Since we know that $P(A)=0.42$ to $2$ decimal places, we can calculate $P({A}^{'})$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A)+P({A}^{'}) & =1 \\ P({A}^{'}) & =1-P(A) \\  & =1-0.42 \\  & =0.58.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem: Three balls are drawn from a bag that contains $5$ white balls and $4$ black balls. Define $A$ to be the event "at least one white ball is drawn." It is known that $P(A)=0.95$ to $2$ decimal places. To two decimal places, what is the probability of drawing three black balls?
questions.worked_solution:
The event "three black balls are drawn" is the opposite of the event "at least one white ball is drawn."

So, the event "three black balls are drawn" is the complement of $A,$ denoted ${A}^{'}.$

Since we know that $P(A)=0.95$ to $2$ decimal places, we can calculate $P({A}^{'})$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A)+P({A}^{'}) & =1 \\ P({A}^{'}) & =1-P(A) \\  & =1-0.95 \\  & =0.05.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements must be true regarding any tetrahedron? 

I. - It has $4$ congruent faces, each in the form of a right triangle
II. - Exactly $3$ faces meet at each vertex
III. - It has $4$ edges
questions.worked_solution:
![](images/ad/adcc202ad86b782fd153566d6454269dcd50e8f1d9aca37bc42d2266c142ced8.png)

Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. A tetrahedron is a regular polyhedron that 

- consists of $4$ congruent faces, each in the form of an equilateral triangle (not a right triangle), and

- exactly $3$ faces meet at each vertex.

- Statement III is false. Since there are $F=4$ faces, each in the form of an equilateral triangle, we have

$$
S=4\cdot 3=12
$$

sides combined. Now, each edge of the polyhedron is created when two face sides coincide. So, the number of edges of the tetrahedron must be equal to

$$
\frac{S}{2}=\frac{12}{2}=6.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
![](images/95/95c30eab094a24beb6976262167401efa973dbac12781c69d074eb14e12e2743.png)

Consider the picture above. Which of the following is a unit vector that is parallel to $m+n?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we have to find $m+n.$ According to the triangle law of addition, the resultant $m+n$ goes from the tail of $m$ to the head of $n:$ 

![](images/87/87647211f77776c5f5f740c205fafb150eef1b9d3ebefb82df73a9fdcd953bdb.png)

In $△AHB$, we have $∠AHB={90}^{∘}$, $AH=0.5=\frac{1}{2}$ and $BH=2.$ So, the Pythagorean theorem gives

$$
\begin{aligned}|m+n| & =AB \\  & =\sqrt{A{H}^{2}+B{H}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the magnitude of $m+n$ is $\frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.$ Consequently, the unit vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{1}{|m+n|}\cdot (m+n) \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}(m+n).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify $\frac{{sin}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the numerator of the first term using $1-{cos}^{2}x={sin}^{2}x.$

$$
\frac{{sin}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1=\frac{1-{cos}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1
$$

Next, we factor the numerator of the first term as a difference of squares, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{cos}^{2}x}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1 & =\frac{(1-\operatorname{cos}x)(1+\operatorname{cos}x)}{1-\operatorname{cos}x}-1 \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(1-\operatorname{cos}x)}(1+\operatorname{cos}x)}{\cancel{1-\operatorname{cos}x}}-1 \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}x}{1}-1 \\  & =1+\operatorname{cos}x-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}x\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify ${(\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{6}))}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we expand the parenthesis and use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{6}))}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{6})+2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{6})+{cos}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =[{sin}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{6})+{cos}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{6})]+2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =1+2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{6})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x=\operatorname{sin}2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the above, we get

$$
2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{6})=\operatorname{sin}(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})=\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{3}).
$$

Therefore,

$$
{(\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{6}))}^{2}=1+2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{6})=1+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{3}).
$$

questions.problem: $\frac{\operatorname{sin}{80}^{∘}\operatorname{tan}{40}^{∘}-1}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}}=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}2x=2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x
$$

Substituting $x={40}^{∘}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}(2\cdot {40}^{∘}) & =2\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}({80}^{∘}) & =2\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can rewrite the given expression using the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}{80}^{∘}\operatorname{tan}{40}^{∘}-1}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}}{\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}}-1}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{2{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-1}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-1+{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-(1-{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘})}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}}\end{aligned}
$$

Using  the Pythagorean identity in the form ${cos}^{2}{40}^{∘}=1-{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-(1-{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘})}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} & =\frac{{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-{cos}^{2}{40}^{∘}}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘})(\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}-\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘})}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘})}(\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}-\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘})}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}}} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}-\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the exact value of $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{8})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{5\pi }{8}).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x=\operatorname{sin}2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{5\pi }{8}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{8})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{5\pi }{8}) & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{8})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{5\pi }{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}(2\cdot \frac{5\pi }{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{8})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{5\pi }{8})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the exact value of ${(\operatorname{sin}({165}^{∘})-\operatorname{cos}({165}^{∘}))}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we expand the parenthesis and use the Pythagorean identity.

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\operatorname{sin}({165}^{∘})-\operatorname{cos}({165}^{∘}))}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}({165}^{∘})-2\operatorname{sin}({165}^{∘})\operatorname{cos}({165}^{∘})+{cos}^{2}({165}^{∘}) \\  & =[{sin}^{2}({165}^{∘})+{cos}^{2}({165}^{∘})]-2\operatorname{sin}({165}^{∘})\operatorname{cos}({165}^{∘}) \\  & =1-2\operatorname{sin}({165}^{∘})\operatorname{cos}({165}^{∘})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x=\operatorname{sin}2x
$$

Substituting $x={165}^{∘}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}({165}^{∘})\operatorname{cos}({165}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{sin}(2\cdot {165}^{∘}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}({330}^{∘}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we obtain

$$
1-2\operatorname{sin}({165}^{∘})\operatorname{cos}({165}^{∘})=1-(-\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{(\operatorname{sin}({165}^{∘})+\operatorname{cos}({165}^{∘}))}^{2}=\frac{3}{2}.
$$

questions.problem: $10\operatorname{sin}({75}^{∘})\operatorname{cos}({75}^{∘})\operatorname{csc}({150}^{∘})=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x=\operatorname{sin}2x
$$

Substituting $x={75}^{∘}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}({75}^{∘})\operatorname{cos}({75}^{∘}) & =\operatorname{sin}(2\cdot {75}^{∘})=\operatorname{sin}({150}^{∘})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can rewrite the given expression using the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}10\operatorname{sin}({75}^{∘})\operatorname{cos}({75}^{∘})\operatorname{csc}({150}^{∘}) & =5\cdot [2\operatorname{sin}({75}^{∘})\operatorname{cos}({75}^{∘})]\operatorname{csc}({150}^{∘}) \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}({150}^{∘})\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}({150}^{∘})} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the exact value of $\frac{\operatorname{sec}(\frac{\pi }{8})}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{16})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{16})}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x=\operatorname{sin}2x
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{16}$ into the above, we get

$$
2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{16})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{16})=\operatorname{sin}(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{16})
$$

which simplifies as

$$
2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{16})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{16})=\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{8}).
$$

Now, we can rewrite the given expression using the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sec}(\frac{\pi }{8})}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{16})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{16})} & =\frac{2\operatorname{sec}(\frac{\pi }{8})}{2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{16})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{16})} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sec}(\frac{\pi }{8})}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{8})} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{8})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{8})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the double-angle formula once more with $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$, we can further simplify the above expression: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{8})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{8})} & =\frac{4}{2\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{8})\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{8})} \\  & =\frac{4}{\operatorname{sin}(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8})} \\  & =\frac{4}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{4})} \\  & =\frac{4}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Some drinks of different sizes and flavors were sold during a school party. The two-way frequency table below summarizes the sold drinks.

|  | Soda | Water | Coca-Cola | Fanta | Totals |

| Large | $5$ | $1$ | $7$ | $7$ | $20$ |
| Totals | $11$ | $8$ | $16$ | $15$ | $50$ |

Estimate the probability that a randomly selected sold drink is a small Fanta.
questions.worked_solution:
To estimate the probability that a randomly selected drink is a small Fanta, we

- find the number at the intersection of the row **"Small"** and the column **"Fanta"**, and then

- divide by the total number of data points in the table.

The number at the intersection of the row **"Small"** and the column **"Fanta"** is highlighted in the table below.

Dividing by the total number of data points in the table $(50),$ we get

$$
p=\frac{8}{50}=0.16.
$$

questions.problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(0,-11).$ What are the polar coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we determine $r:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(-11)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{121} \\  & =11\end{aligned}
$$

Since the point $P$ lies on the negative half of $y$-axis, we have $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $(11,\frac{3\pi }{2}).$

questions.problem:
Researchers surveyed students in School A on which superpower they would most like to have. The results of this survey are summarized in the two-way frequency table below.

|  | Flying | Invisibility | Other | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Female | $16$ | $18$ | $12$ | $46$ |
| Male | $28$ | $12$ | $14$ | $54$ |
| Totals | $44$ | $30$ | $26$ | $100$ |

School B has $300$ students. Assuming the distribution of results is the same for both schools, estimate the number of School B students who are male and would choose to fly as their superpower.
questions.worked_solution:
To estimate the number of students who are male and would choose to fly as their superpower, we

- find the number at the intersection of the row **"Male"** and the column **"Flying"**, and then

- divide by the total number of data points at the table.

The number at the intersection of the row **"Male"** and the column **"Flying"** is highlighted in the table below.

|  | Flying | Invisibility | Other | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Female | $16$ | $18$ | $12$ | $46$ |
| Male | $28$ | $12$ | $14$ | $54$ |
| Totals | $44$ | $30$ | $26$ | $100$ |

Dividing this number by the total number of data points in the table $(100),$ we get

$$
p=\frac{28}{100}=0.28.
$$

This represents the estimated probability that a randomly selected School A student is a male and chooses to fly as his superpower.

Finally, to find the estimated number of School B students who are male and would choose to fly as their superpower, we multiply the total number of School B students $(300)$ by the probability above:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =300\cdot p \\  & =300\cdot 0.28 \\  & =84\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following trigonometric equation: 

$$
\operatorname{cot}(2x)=\sqrt{3}
$$

The general solution of this equation can be expressed as 

$$
x={a}^{∘}+n\cdot {90}^{∘},
$$

where $n$ is any integer. Which of the following could be the value of $a?$
questions.worked_solution:
The given equation is equivalent to 

$$
\operatorname{tan}(2x)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

So, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & ={30}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the above equation for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{30}^{∘}}{2}+\frac{n\cdot {180}^{∘}}{2} \\ x & ={15}^{∘}+n\cdot {90}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that $a=15.$

questions.problem: The point $(a,b)$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=\sqrt{x-1}-1?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

To plot $y=\sqrt{x-1}-1,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, we take the graph $y=\sqrt{x}.$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally by $1$ unit to the right and get the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-1}.$ After this transformation, the point $(a,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(a+1,b).
$$

- Finally, we shift the result vertically by $1$ unit down and obtain the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-1}-1.$ After this transformation, the point $(a+1,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(a+1,b-1).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(a,b)$ lies on the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$, we have that $\sqrt{a}=b.$

Now consider the graph of $y=\sqrt{x-1}-1.$ Substituting $x=a+1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{a+1-1}-1 \\  & =\sqrt{a}-1 \\  & =b-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(a+1,b-1)$ must lie on $y=\sqrt{x-1}-1.$

questions.problem: The point $(a,b)$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{3}.$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=2(x+2)^{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

To plot $y=2(x+2)^{3},$ we apply the following steps:

- First, we take the graph $y={x}^{3}.$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally by $2$ units to the left and get the graph of $y=(x+2)^{3}.$ After this transformation, the point $(a,b)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(a-2,b).
$$

- Finally, we stretch the graph by a scale factor of  $2$ parallel to the $y$ -axis and get the graph of  $y=2(x+2)^{3}.$ After this transformation, the point $(a-2,b)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(a-2,2b).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(a,b)$ lies on the graph of $y={x}^{3}$, we have that ${a}^{3}=b.$

Now consider the graph of $y=2(x+2)^{3}.$ Substituting $x=a-2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(a-2+2)^{3} \\  & =2{a}^{3} \\  & =2b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(a-2,2b)$ must lie on $y=2(x+2)^{3}.$

questions.problem: The point  $(0,1)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x+2).$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=-f(x)+2?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

We first find a point corresponding to $(0,1)$ on $y=f(x).$ Then, we find a corresponding point on $y=-f(x)+2:$

- To plot the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x+2).$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally $2$ unit to the right  and get the graph of $y=f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(0+2,1)=(2,1).
$$

- Next, to plot the graph of $y=-f(x)+2,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Then, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(2,1)$ will be mapped  to the point

$$
(2,-(1))=(2,-1).
$$

- Next, we shift the result vertically by $2$ units up and obtain the graph of $y=-f(x)+2.$ After this transformation, the point $(2,-1)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(2,-1+2)=(2,1).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(0,1)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x+2)$, we have that 

$$
f(0+2)=1\,⟹\,f(2)=1.
$$

Now consider the graph of $y=-f(x)+2.$ Substituting $x=2$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-f(2)+2 \\  & =-(1)+2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(2,1)$ must lie on $y=-f(x)+2.$

questions.problem: Consider the equation $\operatorname{tan}2x=1$ for $0\le x<2\pi .$ If the exact solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$ are written in ascending order, what is the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =\frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Solving our equation for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{n\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{4n\pi }{8} \\ x & =\frac{(1+4n)\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$

- Setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{5\pi }{8}$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x=\frac{9\pi }{8}$

- Setting $n=3$ gives $x=\frac{13\pi }{8}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0\le x<2\pi .$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ and ${x}_{4}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{8},\frac{5\pi }{8},\frac{9\pi }{8},\frac{13\pi }{8}.
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{4} & =\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{13\pi }{8} \\  & =\frac{14\pi }{8} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
