questions.problem: $\operatorname{sin}(\theta +{62}^{∘})=$
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the cofunction of $\operatorname{sin}\theta $ is $\operatorname{cos}\theta ,$ and the angle complementary to $\theta +{62}^{∘}$ is

$$
{90}^{∘}-(\theta +{62}^{∘})={90}^{∘}-\theta -{62}^{∘}={28}^{∘}-\theta .
$$

 So we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}(\theta +{62}^{∘})=\operatorname{cos}({90}^{∘}-(\theta +{62}^{∘}))=\operatorname{cos}({28}^{∘}-\theta ).
$$

questions.problem: Consider the equation $\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}(\frac{3x}{2})+1=0$ for ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘}.$ If the exact solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are written in ascending order, what is the numerical value of ${x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}(\frac{3x}{2})+1 & =0 \\ \sqrt{3}\operatorname{tan}(\frac{3x}{2}) & =-1 \\ \operatorname{tan}(\frac{3x}{2}) & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \operatorname{tan}(\frac{3x}{2}) & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We will find the general solution to the equation, and then generate all of the solutions in the required domain.

The general solution to our equation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x}{2} & =-{30}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving our equation for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & =-{60}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘} \\ x & =-\frac{{60}^{∘}}{3}+\frac{n\cdot {360}^{∘}}{3} \\ x & =-{20}^{∘}+n\cdot {120}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘}.$

- Setting $n=1$ gives $x={100}^{∘}$

- Setting $n=2$ gives $x={220}^{∘}$

- Setting $n=3$ gives $x={340}^{∘}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain ${0}^{∘}\le x<{360}^{∘}.$ So, the solutions ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ (written in ascending order) are

$$
x={100}^{∘},{220}^{∘},{340}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, the numerical value of ${x}_{2}+{x}_{3}$ is $220+340=560.$

questions.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, $b=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]$ and $c=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3 \\ 8\end{aligned}].$ Find $a-(b+c).$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute $a-(b+c),$ we just need to perform the required operations with each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}a-(b+c) & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-([\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 3 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -7 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $k\ge 1$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(k+2)!}{(k-1)!}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice the following:

$$
(k+2)!=(k+2)\cdot (k+1)\cdot k\cdot (k-1)!
$$

Then, we cancel the $(k-1)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(k+2)!}{(k-1)!} & =\frac{(k+2)\cdot (k+1)\cdot k\cdot (k-1)!}{(k-1)!} \\  & =\frac{(k+2)\cdot (k+1)\cdot k\cdot \cancel{(k-1)!}}{\cancel{(k-1)!}} \\  & =k(k+1)(k+2)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $n\ge 2$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(n-1)^{2}\,(n-1)!}{(n-2)!}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}(n-1)! & =(n-1)(n-2)!\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can cancel the $(n-2)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n-1)^{2}\cdot (n-1)!}{(n-2)!} & =\frac{(n-1)^{2}\cdot (n-1)\cdot (n-2)!}{(n-2)!} \\  & =\frac{(n-1)^{2}\cdot (n-1)\cancel{(n-2)!}}{\cancel{(n-2)!}} \\  & =(n-1)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A shop sells $10$ fruit flavors and $12$ chocolate flavors of ice cream. How many choices of ice cream are there?
questions.worked_solution:
In order to find the total number of choices, we can use the **rule of sum**:

$$
10+12=22
$$

Therefore, there are $22$ choices of ice cream.

questions.problem: How many possible outcomes are there if a coin is flipped twice, a six-sided die is rolled three times, and a tetrahedral (four-sided) die is rolled once?
questions.worked_solution:
For the coin, there are $2$ outcomes: "Heads" and "Tails".

For the six-sided die, there is a total of $6$ outcomes: $1,2,3,4,5,6.$

For the tetrahedral die, there is a total of $4$ outcomes: $1,2,3,4.$

Using the **rule of product**, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Possible Outcomes} & =\text{Number of outcomes when the coin is flipped the first time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the coin is flipped the second time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the first time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the second time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the third time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the tetrahedral die is rolled the one time} \\  & =2\times 2\times 6\times 6\times 6\times 4 \\  & ={2}^{2}\times {6}^{3}\times 4 \\  & =4\times 216\times 4 \\  & =3\,456.\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are $3\,456$ possible outcomes.

questions.problem: In an ice cream shop offering twelve flavors of ice cream, half a dozen toppings, and half a dozen syrups, how many combinations are possible when selecting one flavor, one topping, and one syrup?
questions.worked_solution:
For the ice cream flavor, there are $12$ possible choices (a dozen).

For the toppings, there are $6$ possible choices (half a dozen).

For the syrups, there are also $6$ possible choices (half a dozen).

Using the **rule of product**, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Possible Choices} & =\text{Choices for the ice cream flavor} \\  & \times \text{Choices for the topping} \\  & \times \text{Choices for the syrup} \\  & =12\times 6\times 6 \\  & =12\times {6}^{2} \\  & =432.\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are $432$ possible choices.

questions.problem: What is the diameter of a circle if its area is $\frac{9}{25}\pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of a circle is $A=\pi {r}^{2}$, where $r$ is the radius. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{9}{25}\pi  & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{9}{25}\cancel{\pi } & =\cancel{\pi }{r}^{2} \\ r & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} \\ r & =\frac{3}{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the diameter is

$$
d=2\cdot r=2\cdot \frac{3}{5}=\frac{6}{5}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the value of $\operatorname{csc}({90}^{∘}).$
questions.worked_solution:
The angle ${90}^{∘}$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](images/ed/edad8c833f65c54453fe40a326cbf9394c263213934447872b530a8e4fb86de1.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${90}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}({90}^{∘})=1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}({90}^{∘})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}({90}^{∘})}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{csc}({90}^{∘})=1.$

questions.problem: Find the value of $\operatorname{csc}({0}^{∘}).$
questions.worked_solution:
The angle ${0}^{∘}$ is a quadrantal angle. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](images/79/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${0}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}({0}^{∘})=0.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}({0}^{∘})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}({0}^{∘})}=\frac{1}{0}.
$$

However, division by zero is undefined. Therefore, $\operatorname{csc}({0}^{∘})$ is undefined.

questions.problem: Find the value of $\operatorname{tan}\pi +\operatorname{cot}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
The angles $\pi $ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](images/79/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

Let's first consider the angle $\pi .$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\pi $ corresponds to the point $(-1,0).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}\pi =-1.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}\pi =0.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}\pi =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\pi }{\operatorname{cos}\pi }=\frac{0}{-1}=0.
$$

Now, let's consider the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cot}(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{0}{1}=0.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{tan}\pi +\operatorname{cot}(\frac{\pi }{2})=0+0=0.
$$

questions.problem: Find the value of $\operatorname{sec}0+\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
The angles $0$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](images/79/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

- Let's first consider the angle $0.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $0$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$  Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}0=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}0=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}0}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

- Now, let's consider the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$  Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{sec}0+\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1+1=2.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that  ${a}_{n}=(2n)!$ for $n\ge 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. - $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1$
II. - ${a}_{n}$ is an increasing sequence
III. - ${a}_{n}$ is a decreasing sequence
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is a positive sequence defined for $n\ge 1,$ and that

$$
L=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}.
$$

Then,

- if $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *increasing,* and

- if $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *decreasing.*

Notice that, in this case, ${a}_{n}=(2n)!$ is positive for all $n\ge 1.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement.

- Statement I is true. Computing the ratio $L,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}} & =\frac{(2(n+1))!}{(2n)!} \\  & =\frac{(2n+2)!}{(2n)!} \\  & =\frac{(2n+2)\cdot (2n+1)\cdot (2n)!}{(2n)!} \\  & =\frac{(2n+2)\cdot (2n+1)\cdot \cancel{(2n)!}}{\cancel{(2n)!}} \\  & =(2n+2)(2n+1) \\  & \ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, whereas statement III is false. Since $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ we can conclude that the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is increasing.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Given that  ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}$ for $n\ge 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. - $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1$
II. - ${a}_{n}$ is an increasing sequence
III. - ${a}_{n}$ is a decreasing sequence
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is a positive sequence defined for $n\ge 1,$ and that

$$
L=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}.
$$

Then,

- if $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *increasing,* and

- if $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *decreasing.*

Notice that, in this case, ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}$ is positive for all $n\ge 1.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement.

- Statement I is false. Computing the ratio $L,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}} & =\frac{(\frac{1}{(n+1)!})}{(\frac{1}{n!})} \\  & =\frac{n!}{(n+1)!} \\  & =\frac{n!}{(n+1)\cdot n!} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{n!}}{(n+1)\cdot \cancel{n!}} \\  & =\frac{1}{n+1} \\  & \le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false whereas statement III is true. Since $0\le L<1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ we can conclude that the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem:
Find the eleventh partial sum of the series
${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(2-2n).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=2-2n.$ If we compute the first few terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =2-2(1)=0 \\ {a}_{2} & =2-2(2)=-2 \\ {a}_{3} & =2-2(3)=-4,\end{aligned}
$$

and we notice that this is an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=-2$ and first term ${a}_{1}=0.$ 

We can compute the $k$th partial sum of an arithmetic series using the formula

$$
{s}_{k}=\frac{k}{2}({a}_{1}+{a}_{k}).
$$

Since ${a}_{11}=2-2(11)=-20,$ we get

$$
{s}_{11}=\frac{11}{2}(0-20)=-110.
$$

So the eleventh partial sum of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(2-2n)$ is equal to $-110.$

${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-2n).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=-2n.$ If we compute the first few terms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =-2(1)=-2 \\ {a}_{2} & =-2(2)=-4 \\ {a}_{3} & =-2(3)=-6,\end{aligned}
$$

and we see that this is an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=-2$ and ${a}_{1}=-2.$ 

We can compute the $k$th partial sum of an arithmetic series using the formula

$$
{s}_{k}=\frac{k}{2}({a}_{1}+{a}_{k}).
$$

Since ${a}_{k}=-2k$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{k} & =\frac{k}{2}(-2+(-2k)) \\  & =-\frac{k(2+2k)}{2} \\  & =-k(1+k).\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the $k$th partial sum of an arithmetic series using the formula

questions.problem:
Determine the third partial sum of the series
${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}={(\frac{3}{4})}^{n}.$ We note that this is a geometric sequence with $r=\frac{3}{4}$ and first term given by

$$
{a}_{1}={(\frac{3}{4})}^{1}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

The $k$th partial sum of a geometric series is given by

$$
{s}_{k}={a}_{1}(\frac{1-{r}^{k}}{1-r}).
$$

Therefore, the third partial sum is

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{3}={\sum }_{n=1}^{3}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot \frac{(1-{r}^{3})}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot \frac{(1-{[\frac{3}{4}]}^{3})}{(1-\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot \frac{(1-\frac{27}{64})}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =3\cdot \cancel{\frac{1}{4}}\cdot \frac{(\frac{37}{64})}{(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})} \\  & =\frac{111}{64}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\sqrt{3}).$ Does it converge or diverge? If it converges, what is the sum of the series?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's compute the first few partial sums:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{1} & =-\sqrt{3} \\ {s}_{2} & =-\sqrt{3}+(-\sqrt{3})=-2\sqrt{3} \\ {s}_{3} & =-\sqrt{3}+(-\sqrt{3})+(-\sqrt{3})=-3\sqrt{3} \\ {s}_{4} & =-\sqrt{3}+(-\sqrt{3})+(-\sqrt{3})+(-\sqrt{3})=-4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the sequence of partial sums, we can see that the formula for the $n$th partial sum is 

$$
{s}_{n}=-\sqrt{3}n.
$$

The sequence of partial sums is divergent:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{s}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }(-\sqrt{3}n)=-\infty 
$$

Therefore, the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\sqrt{3})$ is also divergent.

questions.problem: Consider the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi ).$ Does it converge or diverge? If it converges, what is the sum of the series?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's compute the first few partial sums:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{1} & =\operatorname{sin}(\frac{3\pi }{2})=-1 \\ {s}_{2} & =-1+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{2})=0 \\ {s}_{3} & =0+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{7\pi }{2})=-1 \\ {s}_{4} & =-1+\operatorname{sin}(\frac{9\pi }{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the above, we can see that the sequence of partial sums oscillates between $0$ and $-1$ forever. 

So the limit of the sequence of partial sums does not exist, and therefore the series is divergent.

questions.problem: Consider the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{2}.$ Does it converge or diverge? If it converges, what is the sum of the series?
questions.worked_solution:
The given series is an arithmetic series. Its first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and its $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{n}{2}.
$$

Using the formula for the sum of an arithmetic series, we get the following formula for the $n$th partial sum:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{n} & =\frac{n}{2}({a}_{1}+{a}_{n}) \\  & =\frac{n}{2}(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{n}{2}) \\  & =\frac{n(1+n)}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the limit of the partial sums, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{s}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n(1+n)}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{n}^{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the limit of the sequence of partial sums is infinite, the series is divergent.

questions.problem: Consider the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(n+3).$ Does it converge or diverge? If it converges, what is the sum of the series?
questions.worked_solution:
The given series is an arithmetic series. Its first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=1+3=4,
$$

Its $n$th term is

$$
{a}_{n}=n+3.
$$

Using the formula for the sum of an arithmetic series, we get the following formula for the $n$th partial sum:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{n} & =\frac{n}{2}({a}_{1}+{a}_{n}) \\  & =\frac{n}{2}(4+n+3) \\  & =\frac{n(7+n)}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the limit of the partial sums, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{s}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n(7+n)}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{n}^{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the limit of the sequence of partial sums is infinite, the series is divergent.

questions.problem: Given that ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is divergent, determine all real values of $K$ for which ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(1-K)\cdot {a}_{n}$ is divergent.
questions.worked_solution:
If we multiply the terms of a divergent series by a non-zero constant, the resulting series is divergent.

Therefore, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(1-K)\cdot {a}_{n}
$$

is divergent when

$$
1-K\ne 0\,\Rightarrow \,K\ne 1.

Given that ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is divergent, which of the following statements is true regarding the series ${\sum }_{n=k}^{\infty }{a}_{n},$ where $k$ is a positive integer, and ${a}_{n}$ is well-defined for all $n⩾1?$

I. - It is convergent for $1<k\le 500$
II. - It is divergent for $k>500$
III. - It is convergent for $50<k\le 100$
questions.worked_solution:
Removing the first $k-1$ terms from a divergent series results in a divergent series.

More precisely, assume ${a}_{n}$ is well-defined for $n\ge 1$ and $k\ge 1$ is an integer. Then, we have the following:

*If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is divergent, then ${\sum }_{n=k}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also divergent.*

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Given that ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent, which of the following statements are true?

I. - $-{10}^{500}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent
II. - ${\sum }_{n=25}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is divergent
III. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}-{10}^{500}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is divergent
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the properties of convergent series:

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }K\cdot {a}_{n}=K\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent and ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}$ is convergent.

- If ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is convergent, then ${\sum }_{n=k}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is also convergent.

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement:

- Statement I is true. Any constant multiple of a convergent series gives a convergent series.

- Statement II is false. Removing a finite number of terms from a convergent series gives a convergent series.

- Statement III is false. The sum of two convergent series is convergent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $(n-4)!$ for any $n\ge 5?$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the definition of factorial, we have

$$
(n-4)!=(n-4)\cdot (n-5)\cdot (n-6)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1.
$$

Now, applying the factorial definition to all but the first factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(n-4)! & =(n-4)\cdot \overset{(n-5)!}{\overset{⏞}{(n-5)\cdot (n-6)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =(n-4)\cdot (n-5)!\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is $\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})$ expressed in terms of a reference angle?
questions.worked_solution:
We wish to express $\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})$ in terms of $\operatorname{tan}{\theta }_{R},$ where ${\theta }_{R}$ is the reference angle corresponding to the angle $\theta =-\frac{17\pi }{12}.$ 

To express $\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})$ in terms of $\operatorname{tan}{\theta }_{R},$ we proceed as follows: 

- **Step 1**: Find the corresponding coterminal angle that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$ We do this by adding integer multiples of $2\pi $ until we get our desired angle:

$$
-\frac{17\pi }{12}+2\pi =\frac{7\pi }{12}\,✓
$$

Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})=\operatorname{tan}(\frac{7\pi }{12}).
$$

![](images/78/7828b40e3fba874611bb9c20e38e0880375aec389ae8ec646d92ea1e1b276883.png)

- **Step 2**: Compute the reference angle. Since $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{12}$ is in the $2$nd quadrant, the reference angle is

$$
{\theta }_{R}=\pi -\frac{7\pi }{12}=\frac{5\pi }{12}.
$$

- **Step 3**: Determine the correct sign. The tangent function is negative $(-)$ in the second quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})=-\operatorname{tan}{\theta }_{R}=-\operatorname{tan}(\frac{5\pi }{12})
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\operatorname{tan}(-\frac{17\pi }{12})=-\operatorname{tan}(\frac{5\pi }{12}).
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=10$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.25$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=10.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.25.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{10}{1-(-0.25)} \\  & =\frac{10}{1+0.25} \\  & =\frac{10}{1.25} \\  & =\frac{1\,000}{125} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OP}=p=i+2j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OQ}=q=-2i+j.\end{aligned}

Expressing $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =q-p \\  & =(-2i+j)-(i+2j) \\  & =-3i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\overset{\to }{PQ}| & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+1} \\  & =\sqrt{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8\end{aligned}].$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $2a+b$ and points the same direction.

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{2a+b}{|2a+b|}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's compute the sum:

$$
\begin{aligned}2a+b & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+5 \\ 4+8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$

$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following series are convergent?

I. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\sqrt[3]{{n}^{2}}}$
II. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3{n}^{4}}$
III. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5\sqrt[3]{n}}{\sqrt{n}}$
questions.worked_solution:
We analyze each series in turn.

- First, we look at ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\sqrt[3]{{n}^{2}}}.$ Rewriting this series gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\sqrt[3]{{n}^{2}}} & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{n\cdot {n}^{2/3}} \\  & =2{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{5/3}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{5}{3}.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

- For the second series, we have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3{n}^{4}}=\frac{1}{3}\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{4}}
$$

 
which is a $p$-series with $p=4.$ Since $p>1,$ the series is convergent.

- For the third series, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5\sqrt[3]{n}}{\sqrt{n}} & =5{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{n}^{1/3}}{{n}^{1/2}} \\  & =5{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{1/6}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{1}{6}.$ Since $p\le 1,$ the series diverges by the $p$-series test.

Hence, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:

II. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{4{n}^{3}}$
III. - ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt[5]{{n}^{3}}}$
questions.worked_solution:
We analyze each series in turn.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3n}{\sqrt[4]{{n}^{5}}} & =3{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{n}{{n}^{5/4}} \\  & =3{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{1/4}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{1}{4}.$ Since $p\le 1,$ the series diverges by the $p$-series test.

- For the second series, we have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{4{n}^{3}}=\frac{5}{4}\cdot {\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{3}}
$$

 
and this is a $p$-series with $p=3.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

- For the third series, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt[5]{{n}^{3}}} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{n}^{1/2}}{{n}^{3/5}} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{1/10}},\end{aligned}
$$

and this is a $p$-series with $p=\frac{1}{10}.$ Since $p\le 1,$ the series divergess by the $p$-series test.

Hence, the correct answer is "II only."

and this is a $p$-series with $p=2.$ Since $p>1,$ the series converges by the $p$-series test.

questions.problem: For which values of $q$ does the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{q-2}}$ converge?
questions.worked_solution:
A $p$-series is any series that takes the form

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{p}},
$$

where $p$ is a constant. The $p$-series test states that

- if $p>1,$ then the series converges, while

- if $p\le 1,$ then the series diverges.

Comparing our series to the $p$-series, we have

$$
p=q-2.
$$

According to the $p$-series test, the given series converges if

$$
q-2>1\,⟹\,q>3.
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent for all $q>3.$

questions.problem: For which values of $q$ does the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2-3q}}$ converge?
questions.worked_solution:
A $p$-series is any series that takes the form

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{p}},
$$

where $p$ is a constant. The $p$-series test states that

- if $p>1,$ then the series converges, while

- if $p\le 1,$ then the series diverges.

Comparing our series to the $p$-series, we have

$$
p=2-3q.
$$

According to the $p$-series test, the given series converges if

$$
2-3q>1\,⟹\,q<\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent for all $q<\frac{1}{3}.$

questions.problem:
If
$D=[\begin{aligned}2x & 6 \\ 2x & x-2\end{aligned}]$
and $det(D)=-32$, what is the value of $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
For a $2\times 2$ matrix, the determinant is given by the formula

$$
|\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}|=ad-bc.
$$

Using the formula, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & =|\begin{aligned}2x & 6 \\ 2x & x-2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2x\cdot (x-2)-6\cdot 2x \\  & =2{x}^{2}-16x\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(D)=-32$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(D) & =-32 \\ 2{x}^{2}-16x & =-32 \\ 2{x}^{2}-16x+32 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-8x+16 & =0 \\ (x-4)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =4\end{aligned}
$$

For our function, the minimum value reached by the function is $h(x)=-4.$

![](images/f7/f76f7203f1ba17f8148bbc1140420034a631f46e6995a3bda5453ec3fd9a6f55.png)

Therefore, the global minimum is ${h}_{min}=-4.$ The function reaches this value when $x=1,$ so the global minimum point is $(1,-4).$

We find $(f+g)(x)$ by adding the two functions:

$$
\begin{aligned}(f+g)(x) & =(3\sqrt{x+1})+(3x-2) \\  & =3x+3\sqrt{x+1}-2\end{aligned}
$$

The notation $(f/h)(x)$ means the quotient of the functions $f(x)$ and $h(x).$ 

To evaluate $(f/h)(4),$ we need to divide $f(4)$ by $h(4).$

Earlier, we found the following values:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & =3\sqrt{5} \\ h(4) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
(f/h)(4)=\frac{f(4)}{h(4)}=\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{3}=\sqrt{5}.
$$

The expression $(f∘h)(4)$ is equivalent to $f(h(4)).$

Previously, we found that 

$$
h(4)=3.
$$

Then, we substitute $x=3$ into $f(x).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(h(4)) & =f(3) \\  & =3\sqrt{3+1} \\  & =3\cdot \sqrt{4} \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we graph the function $g(x)=3x-2.$

![](images/47/47eb01a66773e5cf2b223cc3f8f4ff02caa424170a8e090ec0b1e45ed6d69741.png)

Then, we find the lowest and highest $y$-values in the graph over the domain $x\in [0,2].$

* The lowest $y$ value is $-2.$ This occurs at the point $(0,-2).$

* The highest $y$ value is $4.$ This occurs at the point $(2,4).$

The function covers all the $y$-values between $-2$ and $4,$ including the endpoints.

Therefore, the range is $-2\le y\le 4,$ which can also be written as 

$$
-2\le g(x)\le 4.
$$

If $r$ is the inverse of $g,$ then 

$$
r(g(x))=x.
$$

To find $r(g(x)),$ we write down the function $r$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $g(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(x) & =\frac{1}{3}x+k \\ r(g(x)) & =\frac{1}{3}g(x)+k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $g(x)=3x-2$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(g(x)) & =\frac{1}{3}g(x)+k \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(3x-2)+k \\  & =x-\frac{2}{3}+k\end{aligned}
$$

However, we know that $r(g(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}r(g(x)) & =x \\ x-\frac{2}{3}+k & =x \\ \cancel{x}-\frac{2}{3}+k & =\cancel{x} \\ -\frac{2}{3}+k & =0 \\ k & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\pi $ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\pi }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \,\pi }6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{x}{3}) \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =6\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =3\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's sketch the graph of $y=f(x)=6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{x}{3}).$

![](images/72/72a0459ee5db59562a19961d0304785fb8d46db8be24ad7839d4b8690b0dc835.png)

As $x$ decreases to $-\infty $, the graph oscillates between the values $y=-6$ and $y=6$ indefinitely. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{x}{3})=DNE.
$$

We have the function $f(x)=6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{x}{3}).$ Notice that we are given the length $h$ of the interval. So, the average rate of change of $f$ over this interval is given by

$$
\frac{Δf}{Δx}=\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},
$$

with $a=3\pi .$ Substituting into the formula and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{Δf}{Δx} & =\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \\  & =\frac{f(3\pi +h)-f(3\pi )}{h} \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{1}{3}(3\pi +h))-6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{1}{3}\cdot 3\pi )}{h} \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{sin}(\pi +\frac{h}{3})-6\operatorname{sin}(\pi )}{h} \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{sin}(\pi +\frac{h}{3})-6(0)}{h} \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{sin}(\pi +\frac{h}{3})}{h} \\  & =\frac{6}{h}\operatorname{sin}(\pi +\frac{h}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](images/11/1186087a359b3065400101c7f436c3e885bf937477bdd9f73fbdaab6771aa48a.png)

The graph of the function $g(h)$ is shown above, where

$$
g(h)=\frac{6}{h}\operatorname{sin}(\pi +\frac{h}{3}).
$$

From the graph, what is ${lim}_{h\to \,0}g(h)?$ If the limit does not exist, write "DNE" (without the quotation marks).

${lim}_{h\to \,0}g(h)=$
{{field-1}}

$$
{lim}_{h\to \,{0}^{-}}g(h)=-2.

Similarly, when we approach $h=0$ from the right, the $y$ value approaches $-2.$ So, the right-hand limit is

$$
{lim}_{h\to \,{0}^{+}}g(h)=-2.
$$

Since both the left and right-hand limits exist and are equal to $-2,$ we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{h\to \,0}g(h)=-2.
$$

First, let's attempt to evaluate the limit by direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (3\pi )^{-}}\frac{1}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to (3\pi )^{-}}\frac{1}{6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{x}{3})} \\  & =\frac{1}{6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{3\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{1}{6\operatorname{sin}(\pi )} \\  & =\frac{1}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of $y=\frac{1}{6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{x}{3})}=\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{csc}(\frac{x}{3}).$

![](images/42/42869c56604cbec85b5e4915f77b42e72444b7d9d117e140d9eba56b58c0f131.png)

From the graph, as $x$ approaches $3\pi $ from the left, the values of $y=\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{csc}(\frac{x}{3})$ are positive and increase without bound. Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to (3\pi )^{-}}\frac{1}{f(x)}={lim}_{x\to \,(3\pi )^{-}}\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{csc}(\frac{x}{3})=\infty .
$$

If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,2}\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4}=\frac{2-2}{(2)^{2}-4}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

So, to find the limit, we have to factor the numerator and the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4} & =\frac{x-2}{(x-2)(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x-2}}{\cancel{(x-2)}(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to \,2}\frac{1}{x+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find ${lim}_{x\to \,2}\frac{(x-2)f(x)}{{x}^{2}-4}.$ If the limit does not exist, write "DNE" (without the quotation marks).

${lim}_{x\to \,2}\frac{(x-2)f(x)}{{x}^{2}-4}=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \operatorname{sin}(\frac{2}{3})$
questions.worked_solution:
Previously, we found that 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,2}\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

 

Applying the product rule to the original limit, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}\frac{(x-2)f(x)}{{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to \,2}[\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4}\cdot f(x)] \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,2}\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \,2}\frac{x-2}{{x}^{2}-4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,2}6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{x}{3}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{4})\cdot 6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}(\frac{2}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

In part 1, we found that 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,\pi }f(x)=3\sqrt{3}.
$$

 

Applying the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\pi }\frac{\sqrt{3}f(x)}{(2x+3)^{2}} & =\frac{{lim}_{x\to \,\pi }(\sqrt{3}f(x))}{{lim}_{x\to \,\pi }(2x+3)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, 

* applying the constant multiple rule in the numerator, and 

* the root rule, followed by the sum rule in the denominator, 

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{lim}_{x\to \,\pi }(\sqrt{3}f(x))}{{lim}_{x\to \,\pi }(2x+3)^{2}} & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,\pi }f(x)}{{({lim}_{x\to \,\pi }(2x+3))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\cdot (3\sqrt{3})}{(2\pi +3)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{9}{(2\pi +3)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's start by calculating the first three terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =\frac{f(6\pi \cdot 1+\pi )}{(\sqrt{3})^{1}}=\frac{f(7\pi )}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{7\pi }{3})}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{2\cdot \sqrt{3}}=3 \\ {a}_{2} & =\frac{f(6\pi \cdot 2+\pi )}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=\frac{f(13\pi )}{3}=\frac{6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{13\pi }{3})}{3}=\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{2\cdot 3}=\sqrt{3} \\ {a}_{3} & =\frac{f(6\pi \cdot 3+\pi )}{(\sqrt{3})^{3}}=\frac{f(19\pi )}{3\sqrt{3}}=\frac{6\operatorname{sin}(\frac{19\pi }{3})}{3\sqrt{3}}=\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{2\cdot 3\sqrt{3}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the third partial sum is

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{3} & ={a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+{a}_{3} \\  & =3+\sqrt{3}+1 \\  & =4+\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Previously, we evaluated the first few terms of the series:

$$
{a}_{1}=3,\,{a}_{2}=\sqrt{3},\,{a}_{3}=1
$$

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term, and $r$ is the common ratio.

For the given geometric series, the first term is ${a}_{1}=3,$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

So, using the formula, we find that the sum to infinity is

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{\infty } & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{3}{1-(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})} \\  & =\frac{3}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{\sqrt{3}})} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following expressions are **irrational**?

I. - ${8}^{5}\cdot \sqrt{36}$
II. - ${3}^{20}\cdot 7.0523$
III. - $\sqrt{2}\cdot {2}^{-15}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- the product of two rational numbers is *always* rational:

$$
\text{rational}\times \text{rational}=\text{rational}
$$

- the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is *always* irrational:

$$
\text{rational}\times \text{irrational}=\text{irrational}
$$

- the product of two irrational numbers is *sometimes* rational and *sometimes* irrational.

With that in mind, let's examine the statements.

- Expression I is rational. Notice that $\sqrt{36}=6$ is a rational number. The number ${8}^{5}$ is rational too. So, their product must be rational.

- Expression II is rational. Since both ${3}^{20}$ and $7.0523$ are rational, their product must be rational.

- Expression III is irrational. Since $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational and ${2}^{-15}$ is rational, their product must be irrational.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem: If $-\frac{10tx}{7}=\frac{5}{2},$ then $x=$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate $x.$ To do this, we first cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{10tx}{7} & =\frac{5}{2} \\ \frac{-10tx}{7} & =\frac{5}{2} \\ 2\cdot (-10tx) & =7\cdot 5 \\ -20tx & =35\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $-20t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-20tx & =35 \\ \frac{-20tx}{-20t} & =\frac{35}{-20t} \\ \frac{\cancel{-20t}x}{\cancel{-20t}} & =\frac{35}{-20t} \\ x & =-\frac{35}{20t}\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the right-hand side as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{5\cdot 7}{5\cdot 4t} \\ x & =-\frac{\cancel{5}\cdot 7}{\cancel{5}\cdot 4t} \\ x & =-\frac{7}{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If $\frac{ab-b}{8}=\frac{a-3}{2},$ then $a=$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to isolate all terms with $a$ on one side of the equation. To do this, we first cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{ab-b}{8} & =\frac{a-3}{2} \\ 2\cdot (ab-b) & =8\cdot (a-3) \\ 2ab-2b & =8a-24\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract $8a$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2ab-2b & =8a-24 \\ 2ab-2b-8a & =8a-24-8a \\ 2ab-2b-8a & =-24\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we add $2b$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2ab-2b-8a & =-24 \\ 2ab-2b-8a+2b & =2b-24 \\ 2ab-8a & =2b-24\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that all terms containing $a$ are on the left-hand side, and all terms independent of $a$ are on the right-hand side.

Then, we factor out $a$ from the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2ab-8a & =2b-24 \\ a(2b-8) & =2b-24\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $(2b-8)$ to isolate $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(2b-8) & =2b-24 \\ \frac{a\cancel{(2b-8)}}{\cancel{2b-8}} & =\frac{2b-24}{2b-8} \\ a & =\frac{2b-24}{2b-8} \\ a & =\frac{2(b-12)}{2(b-4)} \\ a & =\frac{b-12}{b-4}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** This result assumes that $b-4\ne 0.$

questions.problem: Calculate the percentage error obtained when approximating the value of $(1.1)^{5}$ using the first three terms of the binomial expansion of $(1+x)^{5}$ in ascending powers of $x.$ Round your final percentage error to two decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that when $n$ is a positive integer, 

$$
(1+x)^{n}=1+nx+\frac{1}{2!}n(n-1){x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{n}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1+x)}^{5} & =1+5x+\frac{1}{2!}\cdot 5\cdot 4\cdot {x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{n} \\  & =1+5x+10{x}^{2}+⋯+{x}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for small $x,$ we have

$$
{(1+x)}^{5}\approx 1+5x+10{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, we substitute $x=0.1$ into the above approximation of $(1+x)^{5}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(1.1)^{5} & =(1+0.1)^{5} \\  & \approx 1+5(0.1)+10(0.1)^{2} \\  & =1+5(0.1)+10(0.01) \\  & =1+0.5+0.1 \\  & =1.6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using a calculator, we can compute the percentage error, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}%\,error & =\frac{\text{amount of error}}{\text{exact value}}\times 100 \\  & =\frac{|(1.1)^{5}-1.6|}{(1.1)^{5}}\times 100 \\  & \approx 0.65%\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

questions.problem: Simplify $2\sqrt[3]{5}+2\sqrt{6}+7\sqrt[3]{40}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we use the product rule for radicals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{40} & =\sqrt[3]{8\cdot 5}=\sqrt[3]{8}\cdot \sqrt[3]{5}=2\sqrt[3]{5} & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt[3]{5}+2\sqrt{6}+7\sqrt[3]{40} & = \\ 2\sqrt[3]{5}+2\sqrt{6}+7(2\sqrt[3]{5}) & = \\ 2\sqrt[3]{5}+2\sqrt{6}+14\sqrt[3]{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can combine the two $\sqrt[3]{5}$ terms together:

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt[3]{5}+2\sqrt{6}+14\sqrt[3]{5} & = \\ 2\sqrt{6}+(2\sqrt[3]{5}+14\sqrt[3]{5}) & = \\ 2\sqrt{6}+(2+14)\sqrt[3]{5} & = \\ 2\sqrt{6}+16\sqrt[3]{5} & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:

The residual plot above was constructed after fitting a linear regression model on a set of bivariate numerical data $(x,y).$
Which of the following statements are true?

I. - When $x=8,$ the regression equation overestimates the value of $y.$
II. - The residuals appear to be randomly scattered about the horizontal axis (there are no obvious trends).
III. - This linear regression is probably a good fit for the data.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The residual equals the actual value minus the estimated value:

$$
\text{Residual}=\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated}
$$

 
From the plot, the residual at $x=8$ is negative. So, we have that $\text{Actual}<\text{Estimated},$ and therefore the model overestimates  this data point.

- Statement II is false. The plot shows the residuals tend to decrease as $x$ increases. So, there is a trend, as shown below.

- Statement III is false. Since the residuals are *not* randomly scattered above and below the horizontal axis, our regression line is *not* a good fit for the given data.

questions.problem: A particle starts moving from the point with position vector $4i\,\text{cm},$ with an acceleration of $(-2i+3j)\,{\text{cm/s}}^{2}$ and an initial velocity of $(2i+j)\,\text{cm/s}.$ Find the distance from the particle to the origin after $2$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
If a particle moves with constant acceleration $a,$ the position vector of the particle at time $t$ can be found using

$$
r={r}_{0}+ut+\frac{1}{2}a{t}^{2},
$$

 

where ${r}_{0}$ is the initial position of the particle and $u$ is its initial velocity.

In our case, we have

$$
{r}_{0}=4i,\,u=2i+j,\,a=-2i+3j.
$$

Therefore, the position vector of the particle after $t=2\,\text{s}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =(4i)+(2i+j)(2)+\frac{1}{2}(-2i+3j)(2)^{2} \\  & =(4i)+(4i+2j)+2(-2i+3j) \\  & =(8i+2j)+(-4i+6j) \\  & =(4i+8j)\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance from the particle to the origin at this time is

$$
\begin{aligned}|r| & =|4i+8j| \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+64} \\  & =\sqrt{80} \\  & =4\sqrt{5}\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}.$  The derivative of this function for $x\in (0,\pi )$ is given by

$$
{y}^{'}=\frac{g(x)\operatorname{sin}x+h(x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x)+h(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x} \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}x.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}y & =\operatorname{ln}(({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}x) \\ \operatorname{ln}y & =\operatorname{ln}(({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2})+\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{sin}x) \\ \operatorname{ln}y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}+6x)+\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{sin}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}+6x)+\operatorname{ln}(\operatorname{sin}x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{'} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+6x}\cdot (2x+6)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}x \\ \frac{{y}^{'}}{y} & =\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{'}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =y(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}x) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}x}{\operatorname{sin}x}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}x}(\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}x}{({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{sin}x}) \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}x|}{\operatorname{sin}x}\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Given that $x\in (0,\pi ),$ then $|\operatorname{sin}x|=\operatorname{sin}x,$ so the fraction $\frac{|\operatorname{sin}x|}{\operatorname{sin}x}$ simplifies to $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)+h(x)=x+3+{x}^{2}+6x={x}^{2}+7x+3.
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{3{n}^{n}}{(1+n)^{n}}.$ According to the root test, does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{3{n}^{n}}{(1+n)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{3{n}^{n}}{(1+n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt[n]{3}\,n}{1+n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt[n]{3}\,n}{n(\frac{1}{n}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt[n]{3}}{(\frac{1}{n}+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{0+1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{3}=1.
$$

Since $L=1,$ the root test gives no conclusion.

questions.problem: $\operatorname{sin}(x+\frac{2\pi }{3})=$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}u\operatorname{cos}v+\operatorname{cos}u\operatorname{sin}v
$$

Applying the sum formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v=\frac{2\pi }{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}(x+\frac{2\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}(\frac{2\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{sin}(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}x\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\operatorname{cos}x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}x}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}x}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}x-\operatorname{sin}x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\operatorname{cos}(x+\frac{\pi }{2})=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the sum formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}(u+v)=\operatorname{cos}u\operatorname{cos}v-\operatorname{sin}u\operatorname{sin}v
$$

Applying the sum formula for cosine with $u=x$ and $v=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{cos}x\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}x\cdot 0-\operatorname{sin}x\cdot 1 \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Simplify $\sqrt{18{v}^{7}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first write $18{v}^{7}$ as the product $9{v}^{6}\cdot 2v$ which contains a perfect square $(9{v}^{6}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{18{v}^{7}} & = \\ \sqrt{9{v}^{6}\cdot 2v} & \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we separate the product into two separate radicals:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{9{v}^{6}\cdot 2v} & = \\ \sqrt{{(3{v}^{3})}^{2}\cdot 2v} & = \\ \sqrt{{(3{v}^{3})}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2v} & \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the radical containing the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{(3{v}^{3})}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2v} & = \\ |3{v}^{3}|\cdot \sqrt{2v} & = \\ |3|\cdot |{v}^{3}|\cdot \sqrt{2v} & = \\ 3|v{|}^{3}\sqrt{2v}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Complete the square on the quadratic expression ${x}^{2}-12x+28.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the coefficient of the linear term as a product with $2$ as a factor:

$$
{x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+28
$$

Now, here's the trick. We *add* and *then subtract* ${6}^{2},$ writing the constant term $28$ last:

$$
{{x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}}_{⏟}-\,{6}^{2}+28
$$

The first three terms form a perfect square, which we factor as follows:

$$
(x-6)^{2}-{6}^{2}+28
$$

Finally, evaluating the last two terms, we get

$$
(x-6)^{2}-8.
$$

questions.problem:
Given the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following transformations in the order given:

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $8$ parallel to the $y$-axis

- Stretch it by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $x$-axis

- Translate it to the left by $10$ units

What is the final function expression after applying all the transformations?
questions.worked_solution:
To find the expression, let's apply each of the transformations in turn.

- Stretching the graph of $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $8$ parallel to the $y$-axis is equivalent to multiplying the function expression by $8.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

$$
y=8f(x).
$$

- Stretching the graph of $y=8f(x)$ by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $x$-axis is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $\frac{1}{5}x.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

$$
y=8f(\frac{1}{5}x)=8f(\frac{x}{5}).
$$

- Translating the graph of $y=8f(\frac{x}{5})$ by $10$ units to the left is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $(x+10).$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

$$
y=8f(\frac{1}{5}(x+10))=8f(\frac{x}{5}+2).
$$

Therefore, the final function expression is $y=8f(\frac{x}{5}+2).$

Recall that the horizontal asymptote of $y={e}^{x-a}+b$ is $y=b.$

Substituting $(5,4)$ into the equation of the curve, we get

questions.worked_solution:
We have to solve $h(x)=5,$ or equivalently, $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3=5.$

First, we isolate the term $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}$ by subtracting $3$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3 & =5 \\ \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we isolate the square root by multiplying by $\frac{3}{2}$ on both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x} & =2 \\ \sqrt{x} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the square root is isolated, we can proceed as usual. Squaring both sides of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =3 \\ (\sqrt{x})^{2} & ={3}^{2} \\ x & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check the result by plugging it into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{9}+3 & \overset{?}{=}5 \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot 3+3 & \overset{?}{=}5 \\ 2+3 & =5\,\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The value $x=9$ satisfies the original equation, so we can accept it as a solution.

Therefore, the solution to $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3=5$  is $x=9.$

questions.problem: The antiderivative of $\sqrt[3]{x}$ equals{{field-1}} $+\,\text{ }C$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $\sqrt[3]{x}={x}^{1/3}$, we can apply the power rule with $n=\frac{1}{3}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{1/3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{1/3+1}}{(\frac{1}{3}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4/3}}{(\frac{4}{3})}+C \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{4/3}}{4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

questions.problem:
Given that  ${a}_{n}=\frac{(2n)!}{{5}^{n}}$ for $n\ge 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. - $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}\ge 1$ for all $n>2$
II. - ${a}_{n}$ is an increasing sequence
III. - ${a}_{n}$ is a decreasing sequence
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is a positive sequence defined for $n\ge 1,$ and that

$$
L=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}.
$$

Then,

- if $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *increasing,* and

- if $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *decreasing.*

Notice that, in this case, ${a}_{n}=\frac{(2n)!}{{5}^{n}}$ is positive for all $n\ge 1.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement.

- Statement I is false. Computing the ratio $L,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}} & =\frac{(\frac{(2n+2)!}{{5}^{n+1}})}{(\frac{(2n)!}{{5}^{n}})} \\  & =\frac{{5}^{n}(2n+2)!}{{5}^{n+1}(2n)!} \\  & =\frac{{5}^{n}\cdot (2n+2)\cdot (2n+1)\cdot (2n)!}{{5}^{n}\cdot 5\cdot (2n)!} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{5}^{n}}\cdot (2n+2)\cdot (2n+1)\cdot \cancel{(2n)!}}{\cancel{{5}^{n}}\cdot 5\cdot \cancel{(2n)!}} \\  & =\frac{(2n+2)(2n+1)}{5} \\  & \ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, whereas statement III is false. Since $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ we can conclude that the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is increasing.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Given that  ${a}_{n}={e}^{2n-1}$ for $n\ge 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. - $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1$
II. - ${a}_{n}$ is an increasing sequence
III. - ${a}_{n}$ is a decreasing sequence
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is a positive sequence defined for $n\ge 1,$ and that

$$
L=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}.
$$

Then,

- if $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *increasing,* and

- if $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *decreasing.*

Notice that, in this case, ${a}_{n}={e}^{2n-1}$ is positive for all $n\ge 1.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement.

- Statement I is true. Computing the ratio $L,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2(n+1)-1}}{{e}^{2n-1}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2n+1}}{{e}^{2n-1}} \\  & ={e}^{2n+1-(2n-1)} \\  & ={e}^{2n+1-2n+1} \\  & ={e}^{2} \\  & \ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, whereas statement III is false. Since $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ we can conclude that the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is increasing.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Given that  ${a}_{n}=\frac{{4}^{n}}{(n!)^{2}}$ for $n\ge 1,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. - $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1$
II. - ${a}_{n}$ is an increasing sequence
III. - ${a}_{n}$ is a decreasing sequence
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is a positive sequence defined for $n\ge 1,$ and that

$$
L=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}.
$$

Then,

- if $L\ge 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *increasing,* and

- if $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ then ${a}_{n}$ is *decreasing.*

Notice that, in this case, ${a}_{n}=\frac{{4}^{n}}{(n!)^{2}}$ is positive for all $n\ge 1.$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement.

- Statement I is true. Computing the ratio $L,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}} & =\frac{(\frac{{4}^{n+1}}{((n+1)!)^{2}})}{(\frac{{4}^{n}}{(n!)^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{{4}^{n+1}(n!)^{2}}{{4}^{n}((n+1)!)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{4}^{n+1}(n!)^{2}}{{4}^{n}((n+1)n!)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{4}^{n}\cdot 4\cdot (n!)^{2}}{{4}^{n}\cdot (n+1)^{2}\cdot (n!)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{{4}^{n}}\cdot 4\cdot \cancel{(n!)^{2}}}{\cancel{{4}^{n}}\cdot (n+1)^{2}\cdot \cancel{(n!)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{4}{(n+1)^{2}} \\  & \le 1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false, whereas statement III is true. Since $0<L\le 1$ for all $n\ge 1,$ we can conclude that the sequence ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
The acceleration $a(t)$ of the particle is given by the derivative of the velocity with respect to time. Find the function $a(t).$

$a(t)=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot \operatorname{cot}t$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write

$$
v(t)=4{csc}^{2}(t).
$$

Now, we see that $v(t)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
v=4{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{csc}t.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}=8u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{'}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t} \\  & =8u\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =(8\operatorname{csc}t)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}t\operatorname{cot}t) \\  & =-8{csc}^{2}t\operatorname{cot}t.\end{aligned}
$$

In part 3, we saw that the derivative of a particle's velocity with respect to time gives its acceleration.

To differentiate ${v}_{2}(t),$ we require the product rule. Let $g(t)={t}^{2}$ and $h(t)=\operatorname{sin}(3t).$ Then

$$
{g}^{'}(t)=2t,\,{h}^{'}(t)=3\operatorname{cos}(3t).
$$

We used the chain rule to calculate ${h}^{'}(t).$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2}(t) & ={v}_{2}^{'}(t) \\  & ={g}^{'}(t)\cdot h(t)+g(t)\cdot {h}^{'}(t) \\  & =(2t)(\operatorname{sin}(3t))+({t}^{2})(3\operatorname{cos}(3t)) \\  & =2t\operatorname{sin}(3t)+3{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:

{{field-1}}$\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](images/db/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{6}$ corresponds to the point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2.
$$

Finally, evaluating $v(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ we have

$$
4{csc}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{6})=4{(2)}^{2}=16.

questions.problem:
Another particle has a velocity function given by ${v}_{2}(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}(3t).$ Evaluate the velocity of this particle at $t=\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

${v}_{2}(\frac{5\pi }{6})\,=\,$
{{field-1}}$\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
Evaluating the function ${v}_{2}(t)$ at $t=\frac{5\pi }{6}$, we get

$$
{v}_{2}(\frac{5\pi }{6})={(\frac{5\pi }{6})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{2})
$$

First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\frac{5\pi }{2}$ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5\pi }{2}-2\pi  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{2})=\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](images/db/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$

Therefore, $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{2})=1.$

Finally, 

$$
{v}_{2}(\frac{5\pi }{6})={(\frac{5\pi }{6})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}(\frac{5\pi }{2})=\frac{25{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to \pi /6}{v}_{2}(t) & ={lim}_{t\to \pi /6}{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}(3t) \\  & ={(\frac{\pi }{6})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{36}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $t=\pi $ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}v(t) & ={lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}4{csc}^{2}(t) \\  & =4{csc}^{2}(\pi ) \\  & =4\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}(\pi )} \\  & =\frac{4}{{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{csc}t.$

![](images/36/361e8bf3b622fc2e73be712dae4ec5d189bd15eecbd33c9295db7365bcf71943.png)

As $t$ approaches $\pi $ from the left, the values of $y=\operatorname{csc}t$ are positive and grow without bound. 

Therefore

$$
{lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{csc}t=\infty 
$$

Applying the product and power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}4{csc}^{2}(t) & ={lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}4\cdot {lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}{csc}^{2}(t) \\  & =4\cdot {({lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{csc}(t))}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying by the positive constant $4$ does not change the sign of the limit, so we have

$$
4\cdot {({lim}_{t\to {\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{csc}(t))}^{2}=\infty .
$$

questions.problem: Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+7}{5-x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=\frac{3x+7}{5-x}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=\frac{3y+7}{5-y}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{3y+7}{5-y} \\ x(5-y) & =3y+7 \\ 5x-xy & =3y+7 \\ 5x-7 & =3y+xy \\ 5x-7 & =y(x+3) \\ y & =\frac{5x-7}{x+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{5x-7}{x+3}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=\frac{6-5x}{x+7}.$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{6-7x}{x+5}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following function:

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}-x-3, & x<-3 \\ 0, & x=-3 \\ x+3, & x>-3\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true regarding $f(x)?$

I. - $f(x)$ is defined at $x=-3$
II. - ${lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}f(x)$
III. - ${lim}_{x\to (-3)}f(x)=f(-3)$
IV. - $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-3$
questions.worked_solution:
To test for continuity of $f(x)$ at a point $x=c$, we need to check three conditions:

- Does $f(c)$ exist?

- Does ${lim}_{x\to c}f(x)$ exist?

- Does ${lim}_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)?$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Using the expression for the second branch of the function, we obtain that

$$
f(-3)=0.
$$

So, $f(x)$ is defined at $x=-3.$ $\,\,✓$

- Statement II is true. By calculating the one-sided limits, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}(-x-3) \\  & =-(-3)-3 \\  & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}(x+3) \\  & =(-3)+3 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

As a result:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-3)^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to (-3)^{+}}f(x)
$$

 
Therefore, the limit of $f(x)$ at $x=-3$ exists:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (-3)}f(x)=0\,\,✓
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, we have that ${lim}_{x\to (-3)}f(x)=0=f(-3).$ $\,\,✓$

- Statement IV is true. Since all statements I-III are true, according to the continuity test, the function $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-3.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "All the statements are true."

questions.problem: Given that ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ is divergent, determine all real values of $K$ for which ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(1+{K}^{2})\cdot {a}_{n}$ is divergent.
questions.worked_solution:
If we multiply the terms of a divergent series by a non-zero constant, the resulting series is divergent.

However, the expression $1+{K}^{2}$ is always positive.

questions.problem:
Consider the quadratic equation $\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}+3x+5=0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. - The discriminant of the equation is a perfect square.
II. - The equation has only rational solutions.
III. - The equation has only irrational solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. We have $a=\frac{1}{4},$ $b=3,$ and $c=5.$ So, we calculate the discriminant as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(3)^{2}-4(\frac{1}{4})(5) \\  & =9-5 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

And $4={2}^{2}$ is a perfect square.

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. 

First, notice that our quadratic equation has rational coefficients. And, since the discriminant is a nonzero perfect square, the equation must have two rational solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Consider the quadratic equation $2{x}^{2}+x-4=0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. - The discriminant of the equation is a perfect square.
II. - The equation has only rational solutions.
III. - The equation has only irrational solutions.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have $a=2,$ $b=1,$ and $c=-4.$ So, we calculate the discriminant as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(1)^{2}-4(2)(-4) \\  & =1+32 \\  & =33\end{aligned}
$$

And $33$ is *not* a perfect square.

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true.

First, notice that our quadratic equation has rational coefficients. And, since the discriminant is not a perfect square, the equation must have two irrational solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.problem: The point $(-1,1)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x).$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=3f(x+2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

To plot $y=3f(x+2),$ we apply the following steps: 

- First, we take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Then, shift the graph horizontally by $2$ unit to the left and get the graph of 
$y=f(x+2).$  After this transformation, the point $(-1,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-1-2,1)=(-3,1).
$$

- Finally, we stretch the result by a scale factor of $3$ parallel to the y-axis and get the graph of 
$y=3f(x+2).$ After this transformation, the point $(-3,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(-3,3\cdot 1)=(-3,3).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(-1,1)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x)$, we have that $f(-1)=1.$

Now consider the graph of $y=3f(x+2).$ Substituting $x=-3$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3f(-3+2) \\  & =3f(-1) \\  & =3\cdot 1 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(-3,3)$ must lie on $y=3f(x+2).$

questions.problem: The point  $(0,3)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x-1).$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=f(x)+2?$

$$

- Next, to plot the graph of $y=f(x)+2,$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Next, we shift the result vertically by $2$ units up and obtain the graph of $y=f(x)+2.$ After this transformation, the point $(-1,3)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(-1,3+2)=(-1,5).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(0,3)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x-1)$, we have that 

$$
f(0-1)=3\,⟹\,f(-1)=3.
$$

Now consider the graph of $y=f(x)+2.$ Substituting $x=-1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =f(-1)+2 \\  & =3+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(-1,5)$ must lie on $y=f(x)+2.$

questions.problem: The point  $(2,1)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x-2).$ Which of the following points **must** lie on $y=3-f(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
**Method 1**

We first find a point corresponding to $(2,1)$ on $y=f(x).$ Then, we find a corresponding point on $y=3-f(x):$

- To plot the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x-2).$

- Then, we shift the graph horizontally $2$ units to the left and get the graph of $y=f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(2,1)$ will be mapped to the point

$$
(2-2,1)=(0,1).
$$

- Next, to plot the graph of $y=3-f(x),$ we apply the following steps:

- First, take the graph $y=f(x).$

- Then, we reflect the result across the $x$-axis and get the graph of $y=-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,1)$ will be mapped  to the point

$$
(0,-(1))=(0,-1).
$$

- Next, we shift the result vertically by $3$ units up and obtain the graph of $y=3-f(x).$ After this transformation, the point $(0,-1)$ will be mapped to the point 

$$
(0,-1+3)=(0,2).
$$

**Method 2**

Since the point $(2,1)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x-2)$, we have that 

$$
f(2-2)=1\,⟹\,f(0)=1.
$$

Now consider the graph of $y=3-f(x).$ Substituting $x=0$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3-f(0) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $(0,2)$ must lie on $y=3-f(x).$

questions.problem:
Which of the following numbers lie in the second quadrant in an Argand diagram?

I. - $3-\text{i}$
II. - $-1+2\text{i}$
III. - $-2-4\text{i}$
questions.worked_solution:
- The complex number $3-\text{i}$ has the real part $x=3$ and the imaginary part $y=-1.$ So, it corresponds to the point $(3,-1)$, which lies in the fourth quadrant.

- The complex number $-1+2\text{i}$ has the real part $x=-1$ and the imaginary part $y=2.$ So, it corresponds to the point $(-1,2)$, which lies in the second quadrant.

- The complex number $-2-4\text{i}$ has the real part $x=-2$ and the imaginary part $y=-4.$ So, it corresponds to the point $(-2,-4)$, which lies in the third quadrant.

![](images/fa/fafede137db90419fd849820668f36610ec675aa7a0e8a77d706872e33a149ef.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

We identify the leading term of the polynomial and compute its limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }(2x-{x}^{2}) & ={lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }(-{x}^{2}) \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }({x}^{2}) \\  & =-(\infty ) \\  & =-\infty \end{aligned}
$$

If we attempt to evaluate the limit directly by substituting $x=2,$ we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2}}{2x-{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}}{2(2)-(2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since there is a radical in the numerator, we can evaluate the limit by first multiplying the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2}}{2x-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{2})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})}{(2x-{x}^{2})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{x-2}{x(2-x)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{-(2-x)}{x(2-x)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{\cancel{2-x}}{x\cancel{(2-x)}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}\frac{1}{x(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{2})} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the right Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f(a+iΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}f(0+i\cdot 0.5)\cdot 0.5 \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}0.5f(0.5i) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}0.5(2(0.5i)-{(0.5i)}^{2}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}0.5(i-0.25{i}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the area $A$ as the definite integral of 

$$
f(x)=2x-{x}^{2}
$$

between 

* the lower limit $x=0,$ and 

* the upper limit $x=2.$ 

This gives

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{2}2x-{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

questions.problem: If you deposit $$12,000$ into an account with a $8%$ annual interest rate, compounded quarterly, how many years will it take until there is at least $$18,000$ in the account?
questions.worked_solution:
The compound interest equation states that

$$
\begin{aligned}P & ={P}_{0}{(1+\frac{r}{n})}^{nt}.\end{aligned}
$$

The annual interest is compounded quarterly, and there are $4$ quarters in one year, so $n=4.$ We also have an initial amount of ${P}_{0}=12,000$ and annual rate of $r=0.08.$

To find the number of years it will take until $P\ge 18,000,$ we substitute these values into the formula and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}P={P}_{0}{(1+\frac{r}{n})}^{nt} & \ge 18,000 \\ 12,000{(1+\frac{0.08}{4})}^{4t} & \ge 18,000 \\ (1+0.02)^{4t} & \ge \frac{18,000}{12,000} \\ (1.02)^{4t} & \ge 1.5 \\ log\,({1.02}^{4t}) & \ge log\,(1.5) \\ 4tlog\,(1.02) & \ge log\,(1.5) \\ 4t & \ge \frac{log\,(1.5)}{log\,(1.02)} \\ 4t & \ge 20.475… \\ t & \ge \frac{20.475…}{4}\approx 5.12\end{aligned}
$$

Remember, payments are compounded quarterly, so we must choose either $5$ or $5.25$ years.

- After $5$ years, there is still less than $$18,000$ in the account, because $5<5.12.$

- After $5.25$ years, there will be more than $$18,000$ in the account, since $5.25>5.12.$

Therefore, it will take $5.25$ years ($5$ years and $1$ quarter) until there is at least $$18,000$ in the account.

questions.problem: In terms of $a$ and $b,\,p(10)=\,${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We substitute $x=10$ into the expression for $p(x)$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =a{x}^{2}+bx \\ p(10) & =a(10)^{2}+b(10) \\  & =100a+10b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p(10)=100a+10b.$

In part 1, we found that $p(10)=100a+10b.$ So, we need to solve the equation $100a+10b=4\,800$ for the parameter $b.$

We need to isolate the variable $b.$ To do this, we treat $a$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

First, we subtract $100a$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}100a+10b & =4\,800 \\ 100a+10b-100a & =4\,800-100a \\ 10b & =4\,800-100a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $10:$

$$
\begin{aligned}10b & =4\,800-100a \\ \frac{10b}{10} & =\frac{4\,800-100a}{10} \\ \frac{\cancel{10}b}{\cancel{10}} & =\frac{4\,800}{10}-\frac{100a}{10} \\ b & =480-10a\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $b=480-10a.$

We have the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=480-10a \\ 20b+400a=7\,200\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=480-10a
$$

So, we replace $b$ in the second equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}20b+400a & =7\,200 \\ 20(480-10a)+400a & =7\,200 \\ 9\,600-200a+400a & =7\,200 \\ 9\,600+200a & =7\,200 \\ 200a & =-2\,400 \\ a & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $a=-12$ into $b=480-10a,$ we can then find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =480-10(-12) \\ b & =600\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-12,\,b=600.$

$$

To solve this equation, we want to find a factor pair of the constant term $(600)$ that also adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-50).$ The required factors are $(-20)$ and $(-30).$

$$

questions.problem: If $x=\sqrt[3]{y}+1,$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at the point $(3,8).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt[3]{y}+1) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt[3]{y})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{1/3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{y}^{-2/3}+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{3{y}^{2/3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{-1}=3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}.
$$

Finally, substituting the point $(3,8),$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(3,8)} & =3\sqrt[3]{{y}^{2}}=12.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor ${x}^{2}$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

- The factor $(x+5)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-5$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=-5$ has multiplicity $1.$

questions.problem: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-25x+25$ have multiplicity $1?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. For this polynomial, we can factor by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}-25x+25 \\  & ={x}^{2}(x-1)-25(x-1) \\  & =({x}^{2}-25)(x-1) \\  & =(x+5)(x-5)(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $(x+5)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-5$ has multiplicity $1.$

- The factor $(x-5)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=5$ has multiplicity $1.$

- The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, the roots $x=-5,1,5$ all have multiplicity $1.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+2) & =f(2+1)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =f(3)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =2+(-1) \\ f(4) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fourth term of the sequence is $f(4)=1.$

questions.problem:
Find the solution to the  following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}a-\frac{1}{2}b=1 \\ \frac{1}{5}a+\frac{1}{3}b=3\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To get rid of fractions, we multiply the first equation by $4$ and the second equation by $15,$ as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}a-\frac{1}{2}b=1 & |\times 4 \\ \frac{1}{5}a+\frac{1}{3}b=3 & |\times 15\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}a-2b=4 \\ 3a+5b=45\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the elimination method to solve the system. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-3,$ then we will get a $-3a$ term that can cancel with the $3a$ term in the second equation:

$$
{\begin{aligned}a-2b=4 & |\,\times (-3) \\ 3a+5b=45 & \end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}-3a+6b=-12 \\ 3a+5b=45\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations eliminates the $a$-variable, and allows us to solve for $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{-3a}+6b & =-12 \\ \cancel{3a}+5b & =45 \\ (6b+5b) & =(-12+45) \\ 11b & =33 \\ b & =\frac{33}{11} \\ b & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $b=3$ into the first equation to solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a-2b & =4 \\ a-2(3) & =4 \\ a-6 & =4 \\ a & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system is $a=10,\,b=3.$

questions.problem:
The population $P(t)$ of a city, measured in thousands of people, $t$ years after $2012,$ is given by the expression $P(t)=5{t}^{2}+t.$
